items.readme_text:
# FluxVM [![CI](https://img.shields.io/github/actions/workflow/status/zyvorai/zyvor-fluxvm/ci.yml?branch=main&style=flat-square&labelColor=1d1d1f&label=CI)](https://github.com/zyvorai/zyvor-fluxvm/actions/workflows/ci.yml) [![Security profiles](https://img.shields.io/github/actions/workflow/status/zyvorai/zyvor-fluxvm/security-profiles.yml?branch=main&style=flat-square&labelColor=1d1d1f&label=security%20profiles)](https://github.com/zyvorai/zyvor-fluxvm/actions/workflows/security-profiles.yml) [![DevOps gates](https://img.shields.io/github/actions/workflow/status/zyvorai/zyvor-fluxvm/devops-gates.yml?branch=main&style=flat-square&labelColor=1d1d1f&label=devops%20gates)](https://github.com/zyvorai/zyvor-fluxvm/actions/workflows/devops-gates.yml) [![License: Apache-2.0](https://img.shields.io/github/license/zyvorai/zyvor-fluxvm?style=flat-square&color=0071e3&labelColor=1d1d1f)](LICENSE) [![Last commit](https://img.shields.io/github/last-commit/zyvorai/zyvor-fluxvm/main?style=flat-square&color=0071e3&labelColor=1d1d1f)](https://github.com/zyvorai/zyvor-fluxvm/commits/main) [![Rust: stable](https://img.shields.io/badge/rust-stable-0071e3?style=flat-square&labelColor=1d1d1f&logo=rust&logoColor=white)](https://www.rust-lang.org) [![Book a demo](https://img.shields.io/badge/Book_a_demo-0071e3?style=for-the-badge)](https://zyvor.dev/schedule?utm_source=github&utm_medium=fluxvm&utm_campaign=readme_hero) [![30-day PoC](https://img.shields.io/badge/30--day_PoC-000000?style=for-the-badge)](https://zyvor.dev/poc?utm_source=github&utm_medium=fluxvm&utm_campaign=readme_hero) [![Quickstart](https://img.shields.io/badge/Quickstart_one_JSON_spec-bf5af2?style=for-the-badge)](#quickstart) ### Run real VMs with a real API. **Primary networking: native eBPF.** VM edges require successful attachment by default; nftables is an explicit compatibility mode. Before upgrading configs that omit the dataplane mode, follow the [eBPF upgrade guide](docs/primary-ebpf.md). **One Rust control plane for Firecracker, Cloud Hypervisor, QEMU/KVM and the in-tree FluxVM hypervisor, plus Apple's Virtualization.framework (`vz`) on a Mac.** No libvirtd. No XML. A REST API and a CLI that do the same thing on every backend, with a vsock guest agent instead of SSH. **4 Linux backends + `vz` on Mac, one API** · **No libvirtd, no XML** · **Native KVM, no QEMU** · **SDKs: Python, Go, TypeScript** · **Operator verified on real k3s** [**Quickstart**](#quickstart) · [**Mac cloud**](#your-own-mac-cloud) · [**Proof**](#maturity-whats-real-today) · [**Docs**](docs/index.md) · [**API**](docs/api.md) · [**Talk to Zyvor**](https://zyvor.dev/?utm_source=github&utm_medium=fluxvm&utm_campaign=readme_hero)
--- ## Your own Mac cloud FluxVM runs natively on Apple silicon. Its `vz` backend drives Apple's **Virtualization.framework**, the hypervisor behind macOS's own virtual machines. One Mac gets Linux VMs, macOS guests, agent sandboxes and container VMs over the same REST API, `fluxctl` and MCP server as Linux. A shelf of Mac minis and Mac Studios becomes one fleet: `fluxvm-agent central` places each `vz` request on the Mac that fits. | Built for Mac people | | |---|---| | **Apple silicon native** | Daemon, API and a signed Swift runner per VM (`fluxvm-vz-runner`); no QEMU, no emulation | | **macOS guests** | Install from an IPSW, prepare a template once, clone it with APFS in an instant for Xcode CI (two at a time per Mac, Apple's limit) | | **Rosetta** | x86_64 Linux binaries and `linux/amd64` container images run in arm64 guests | | **APFS clones and warm starts** | Copy-on-write disks and snapshots; a saved VM restores in about 2 s instead of a 10 s boot | | **Shared folders** | `fluxctl run -v ~/src:/mnt/src`: edit on macOS, build in Linux (virtiofs) | | **Keychain sign-in** | `fluxctl signin` keeps a guest password in your login Keychain and types it; the API never returns it | | **launchd** | `fluxctl service install` writes a LaunchAgent, so a headless Mac mini serves VMs after every reboot | | **Agents see the screen** | Screenshots, keyboard and mouse for any `vz` guest, with no Screen Recording permission on the host | | **A throwaway computer per agent task** | An offline sandbox (no network card) is ready in about 4.5 s and forks into four running copies in about 4 s; a local model stays reachable over one vsock port. [Demo](examples/agent-sandbox-demo/README.md) · [Agent sessions](docs/agent-platform/README.md) · [Agents page](https://zyvorai.github.io/zyvor-fluxvm/agents) | ```bash curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/zyvorai/zyvor-fluxvm/main/scripts/install.sh | bash # drives Homebrew, starts the service, checks healthz # or by hand: brew install zyvorai/tap/fluxvm # prebuilt, Apple silicon, macOS 14+ fluxctl run # a throwaway Debian 13 VM and a shell fluxctl sandbox run alpine:3.22 --rm -- echo hi # a container in its own VM ``` The script only runs `brew install zyvorai/tap/fluxvm` and `brew services start`, optionally wires an MCP client (`bash -s -- --client claude-code`), and has `--dry-run` and `--uninstall`; read it first at [`scripts/install.sh`](scripts/install.sh). Step by step, with what was tested (daemon as a service, first VM, MCP client): [Install on a Mac](docs/install-macos.md). From source instead: `xcode-select --install && brew install hivex && cargo build -p fluxctl` (builds and signs the vz runner). [**FluxVM on Mac**](https://zyvorai.github.io/zyvor-fluxvm/mac) · [**Build a Mac cloud**](https://zyvorai.github.io/zyvor-fluxvm/mac-cloud) · [Mac guide](docs/macos.md) · [Mac cloud guide](docs/mac-cloud.md) · [Tenancy, leases and roles](docs/mac-cloud-tenancy.md) · [Run central](docs/mac-cloud-operations.md) · [`fluxctl fleet`](docs/fluxctl-fleet.md) · [SDKs and Terraform](docs/fleet-sdk.md) · [Architecture](docs/macos-architecture.md) Measured on one Apple M4 with macOS 27.2. Multi-Mac fleets are not yet verified on real hardware; see [Native macOS](#native-macos-apple-silicon) below for the full list. ## What's new From the [CHANGELOG](CHANGELOG.md) (0.4.x, current release **0.4.15**) and recent commits: | Feature | What it does | |---|---| | **Docker and Kubernetes on a Mac** | `fluxctl docker up` runs a real `dockerd` in one managed VM with its socket on the Mac (`build`, Compose, bind mounts, networks); `fluxctl kube up` runs k3s in FluxVM VMs (workers, `kube load`, offline installs, Cilium by default) and writes a kubeconfig. Studio's **Platform → Kubernetes** page shows each cluster's nodes and pods, coloured pod logs, a shell in a pod, a traffic graph and a checkpoint timeline ([docker](docs/docker-engine.md), [kubernetes](docs/kubernetes-on-mac.md)) | | **Time travel for a Kubernetes cluster on a Mac** | A checkpoint is the whole running VM, saved in about a second: `kube try -- kubectl apply` then `kube undo`; `kube supervise --auto-checkpoint` and `kube bisect -- TEST` to find the checkpoint where it broke; `kube golden`, `kube reset` and `kube matrix` for clean test runs; `kube chaos` to kill a pod, stop k3s or fill the disk and restore; `kube sleep`, `--idle-sleep`, `--sleep-on-battery`, woken by the first `kubectl` or browser request. Single-node clusters ([guide with diagrams](docs/kubernetes-on-mac.md#time-travel-for-your-cluster)) | | **Kubernetes on a Mac that feels local** | Plain `kubectl` (the cluster is merged into `~/.kube/config`); `http://web.localhost` and, after `kube trust`, `https://web.localhost` for every Service and every Traefik Ingress host; `kube add postgres\|redis\|mysql\|mongodb\|rabbitmq\|nats\|mailpit\|grafana\|redpanda\|qdrant\|meilisearch\|clickhouse` with the usual ports and `kube connect`; `kube forward SERVICE`, a port-forward that survives pod restarts; `kube db-backup` / `db-restore`; `kube dev` (rebuild and restart on save) and `kube sync` (copy files into a pod on save); `kube doctor`, and a notification when a pod crash-loops ([the whole map](docs/kubernetes-on-mac.md#every-command-in-one-place)) | | **Host Metal/MLX inference for offline sandboxes** | `apple.host_gpu` / `fluxctl agent run --host-gpu`: guest `OPENAI_BASE_URL` reaches the host OpenAI-compatible server over vsock (no GPU passthrough). `fluxctl infer status` / `infer serve --stand-in` ([host-inference](docs/host-inference.md)) | | **QMP under a short `run_dir`** | Avoids macOS `sockaddr_un` / `SUN_LEN` failures when the state path is long; sockets live at `run_dir/qmp/.sock`, migration receivers at `run_dir/mr//` ([operations](docs/operations.md#state-layout)) | | **Agent sessions (`fluxctl agent`)** | Enforced filesystem policy, scoped tokens, supervised jobs, approvals, budgets, fork/evaluate/promote — in the published package from 0.4.8 ([session guide](docs/agent-sessions-guide.md)) | | **Agent sandboxes you can fork** | `sandbox_create {"offline": true}`, then `vm_fork`: four running copies in about 4 s, four fixes tested in 0.3 s, the passing one kept ([demo](examples/agent-sandbox-demo/README.md); measured on an M4 mini, copies keep the parent's identity) | | **Fleet platform** | Tenants and 24-hour Mac leases, snapshots and clones, volumes, SSH and port tunnels, SSO and roles, metrics and Prometheus, warm pools, prices and signed webhooks, Go/Python/TypeScript clients and a Terraform provider ([guide](docs/mac-cloud-tenancy.md), [run it](docs/mac-cloud-operations.md); tested against simulated Macs, not a real multi-Mac fleet) | | **FluxVM Studio** | A web UI built into the binaries: the node daemon at `/console/` and fleet central at its own `/console/`, light and dark, ⌘K palette; operators and tenants sign in with their key ([docs/ui.md](docs/ui.md), [install guide](docs/install-macos.md#optional-the-fleet-console)). The previous consoles at `/console/legacy` were removed in 0.4.14 | | **No open registry by accident** | `central` makes a random operator token on first start, keeps it in `/operator-token` (`0600`) and prints it once; `--token` always wins, `--no-auth` is the explicit lab switch ([operations](docs/mac-cloud-operations.md)) | | **FluxMesh personal cloud** | A host-to-host WireGuard overlay across home NAT/CGNAT: overlay IPAM, private DNS (`*.flux`), fail-closed ACLs compiled to Network Fabric, relay fallback, zero-touch enrollment (`fluxctl cloud`) and an optional public HTTPS/HTTP3 edge. Unit-tested, **not yet run on real hosts**, not in the macOS package ([docs/fluxmesh.md](docs/fluxmesh.md)) | | **Install with Homebrew** | `brew install zyvorai/tap/fluxvm`, then `brew services start zyvorai/tap/fluxvm` and `fluxctl mcp install claude-code`; install, service, upgrade and uninstall were run for real ([install guide](docs/install-macos.md)) | | **MCP server for AI agents** | `fluxctl mcp serve` speaks the Model Context Protocol over stdio; read tools by default, `--allow-write` adds VM create, clone, exec, snapshot, delete, power and capture, backups, pools and sandboxes ([docs/mcp.md](docs/mcp.md)) | | **VM fork** | `POST /v1/vms/{id}/fork` / `fluxctl vm fork`: snapshot a running FluxVM-engine VM once and restore N children with a shared read-only memory file and reflinked rootfs | | **VM import** | `POST /v1/images/import` / `fluxctl import-image`: OVA/OVF/VMDK/VHD(X)/qcow2 to raw disks, with offline GuestKit repair of the boot disk for virtio | | **Backups with quiesce** | Guest `fsfreeze` through QGA around the snapshot, plus list, delete and restore-backup | | **Container sandboxes on a Mac** | `"oci": {"image": "alpine:3.22"}` on `POST /v1/sandboxes`, or `fluxctl sandbox run IMAGE -- CMD`, boots the container in its own lightweight `vz` VM: direct kernel boot, a read-only root, uid 65534, no SSH, agent-only exec. Published ports, named volumes, restart policies and health checks; container services in `fluxctl up` stacks (with write-only `secret_env` and `--fleet` placement), `fluxctl import-compose`, and a web dashboard at `/console/`. Docker CLI works via `DOCKER_HOST` against `{run_dir}/docker.sock` ([docs/oci-sandboxes.md](docs/oci-sandboxes.md#docker-cli-docker_host)) | | **GPUs for sandboxes** | `gpus: N` on `POST /v1/sandboxes` passes free VFIO-bound GPUs to a QEMU-backed sandbox; supported in all three SDKs | | **Kairon VM edge, enforced** | Anti-spoof, learn-IP, DNS and SNI allow lists and an egress token bucket loaded into the VM's TC program | | **AppArmor covers Kairon's image cache** | The enforced `fluxctl`/`fluxvm` profiles read Kairon's node image cache and take QEMU's image lock on `storage=shared` disks; without it an image-booted Machine fails `opening base image ... Permission denied` ([profile notes](deploy/apparmor/README.md)) | | **Safer QEMU live migration** | A receiver boots the source's concrete machine type and refuses a host whose QEMU lacks it; the relay closes both sides when either ends; retries restate capabilities; cancelling a finished pre-copy migration resumes the guest ([operations](docs/operations.md), [contract](docs/runtime-boundary.md)). Run live between two hosts with a shared disk, including multifd, post-copy, TLS, cancel-then-retry and a QEMU 8.2 and a QEMU 7.2 source into 10.2: the guest kept running through each move ([script](scripts/test-migration-two-host.sh)). Also zstd compression and auto-converge under a dirtying guest. Not run: a source older than QEMU 7.2 | | **VM-edge packet capture** | A bounded `tcpdump` on the VM's dataplane interface with pcap download | | **Incident bundles** | `POST /v1/vms/{id}/diagnostics` / `fluxctl incident`: one redacted tar.gz with QMP state, cgroup and PSI, the console log, dataplane state and an optional pcap, plus an opt-in QEMU guest memory dump ([docs/diagnostics-bundle.md](docs/diagnostics-bundle.md)) | ## Why FluxVM | When this happens… | FluxVM gives you… | |---|---| | Your automation has to template libvirt XML and talk to libvirtd | A JSON VM spec and a full REST API (`fluxctl serve`), the same on every backend | | Each hypervisor needs its own tooling | QEMU/KVM, Cloud Hypervisor, Firecracker and the in-tree FluxVM hypervisor behind one trait; `"backend":"auto"` picks for you | | Running a command in a guest means SSH keys and a network path | `fluxctl exec -- …` over vsock through the guest agent | | AI agents and CI jobs need a throwaway machine with guard rails | Agent sandboxes: egress ACL on method, host and path, a file change-set, a rootless procbox tier, VM fork and `ttl_seconds` cleanup | | You want Linux VMs without installing QEMU | A pure in-tree KVM engine: SMP verified at 2, 4 and 8 vCPUs, pause and snapshot across every vCPU | | You want VMs in Kubernetes without KubeVirt | A `DisposableVm` CRD and a node-local operator, 9/9 checks on a real k3s cluster | ![Capabilities at a glance: Run, Sandbox, Network, Platform](docs/ux/readme-capabilities.jpg) ## One API. Every hypervisor. A JSON spec in, a running VM out. The same `fluxctl` verbs and the same REST API on every backend, with a vsock guest agent instead of SSH. ```bash sudo fluxctl create --spec examples/qemu.json # boot a VM from a JSON spec fluxctl list # every VM, every backend fluxctl exec -- hostname # run a command over vsock — no SSH fluxctl pause && fluxctl resume # park it instead of rebuilding it fluxctl delete # or set ttl_seconds and walk away ```
Four backends
QEMU/KVM, Cloud Hypervisor, Firecracker and the in-tree FluxVM hypervisor behind one trait. "backend":"auto" picks for you.
Backends 		Native KVM, no QEMU
A pure in-tree KVM engine: SMP verified at 2, 4 and 8 vCPUs, pause and snapshot across every vCPU, and a golden Cloud-init template.
Native KVM 		Agent sandboxes
An egress ACL on method, host and path (HTTPS via opt-in interception), a file change-set, a rootless procbox tier, GPUs for QEMU sandboxes (`gpus: N`), and Python, Go and TypeScript SDKs.
Agent sandboxes
Network Fabric GA
A TC/eBPF VM-edge dataplane with L3/L4 policy, rate limits, security groups and live reconfigure. Native eBPF is the default dataplane; nftables is an explicit compatibility mode.
eBPF dataplane · Network Fabric 		Secure Containers GA
A Pod gets its own guest kernel through containerd runtime-v2, with Sentinel NetworkPolicy. Not a Kata-equivalence claim.
Secure Containers 		Kubernetes
A DisposableVm CRD and a node-local operator, verified on a real k3s cluster, plus a scheduler-native path without KubeVirt.
Operator
--- ## FluxVM vs libvirt/virsh ![FluxVM vs libvirt/virsh: no libvirtd, no XML, a REST API on every backend](docs/ux/readme-vs.jpg) FluxVM is the Zyvor **host-local** replacement for libvirt/virsh VM lifecycle and networking. It is **not** a drop-in for KubeVirt/OpenShift. | libvirt/virsh | FluxVM | |---|---| | `virsh define` + `virsh start` | `fluxctl create` | | `virsh list` / `virsh suspend` / `virsh resume` | `fluxctl list` / `pause` / `resume` | | `virsh console` | `fluxctl serial` (websocket over REST too) | | XML domain definitions | A JSON VM spec (`fluxctl create --spec vm.json`) | | No REST API | A full REST API (`fluxctl serve`) | | `virsh -c qemu+ssh://host` | `fluxctl --server` / `fluxctl context` (REST, bearer token) | | `virsh event` | `fluxctl events -f` (SSE: `/v1/events/stream`) | | libvirtd manages networks | TAP/bridge/netns networking managed directly via netlink | | **Choose libvirt when** | Your tooling is built on its XML, language bindings and ecosystem (virt-manager, virt-install), or you need hypervisors beyond FluxVM's four | The [full command mapping](docs/vs-libvirt.md) covers disks, snapshots, backups, clone and events. --- ## eBPF: the VM network, rewritten inside the kernel [![The VM network, rewritten inside the kernel](docs/ux/ebpf-hero.jpg)](docs/ebpf.md) Every VM's packets are decided by a kernel-verified eBPF program on its own interface, using per-VM maps. That's the default dataplane. - **Policy is a map write.** Live changes take about 100-120 ms p50, cost the same for the first VM and the hundredth, and never open an allow-all window. - **Fewer hops.** The direct datapath cuts the Pod path from 8 devices to 4: -31% latency and +60% small-packet rate in host-forwarding benchmarks. - **Connections survive live migration.** Conntrack moves with the VM and is checked against the destination policy. - **See why packets died.** Attributed drop reasons, flows, stats and on-demand pcaps over REST. It coexists with Cilium and never writes Cilium's maps. [The eBPF dataplane →](docs/ebpf.md) --- ## How it fits together ![A JSON spec in, a running VM out](docs/ux/readme-how-it-works.jpg) - **Architecture:** the control plane, the four backends and the image path — [docs/architecture.md](docs/architecture.md). - **Feature highlights:** every area in one table, with its docs — [docs/index.md](docs/index.md#feature-highlights). - **Kubernetes:** `DisposableVm` and the node-local operator — [docs/kubernetes-operator.md](docs/kubernetes-operator.md). - **FAQ:** is it for you, and the questions people ask first — [docs/faq.md](docs/faq.md). - **Ecosystem:** how FluxVM relates to zyvor-fabric, Ragnarok, h2kvm and GuestKit — [docs/ecosystem.md](docs/ecosystem.md). - **Using FluxVM through Ragnarok:** [docs/ragnarok.md](docs/ragnarok.md), and [zyvor-fabric](docs/zyvor-fabric.md) for the private-cloud control plane. --- ## Quickstart Needs a Linux host with KVM, a Rust toolchain, and a sibling `guestkit` checkout. ```bash git clone https://github.com/zyvorai/zyvor-fluxvm.git && cd zyvor-fluxvm # needs a sibling guestkit checkout sudo ./scripts/bootstrap-host.sh vmbr0 && ./scripts/preflight.sh cargo build --release sudo install -m 0755 target/release/fluxctl /usr/local/bin/fluxctl sudo install -m 0644 config.example.toml /etc/fluxvm.toml sudo fluxctl --config /etc/fluxvm.toml create --spec examples/qemu.json ``` Day-2 verbs, network modes and remote daemons: [Getting started](docs/getting-started.md). ## Use cases Every one maps onto what is implemented today. [All eleven](docs/index.md#use-cases) and [docs/use-cases.md](docs/use-cases.md). - **CI runners that isolate every job:** a VM per job over vsock `exec`, with `ttl_seconds` cleanup. - **AI-agent sandboxes with guard rails:** a microVM or a rootless procbox, an egress ACL and a change-set. - **Linux VMs with no QEMU installed:** the in-tree KVM engine and a golden template, `fluxctl vm-template create native-agent `. - **A golden-image pipeline:** build once with `fluxctl build-image`, reuse through CoW overlays and a signed catalog. - **Kubernetes-native VMs without KubeVirt** and **OCI workloads with a per-Pod guest kernel.** ## Documentation map | Topic | Doc | |---|---| | Every feature area and document | [docs/index.md](docs/index.md) | | Positioning, overview and the exhaustive feature list | [docs/POSITIONING.md](docs/POSITIONING.md) · [docs/PRODUCT_OVERVIEW.md](docs/PRODUCT_OVERVIEW.md) · [FEATURES.md](FEATURES.md) | | REST API, auth/RBAC and the VM JSON contract | [docs/api.md](docs/api.md) | | Day-2 operations | [docs/operations.md](docs/operations.md) | | Host hardening: the AppArmor profile and what it allows | [deploy/apparmor/README.md](deploy/apparmor/README.md) | | Live migration contract and receivers | [docs/runtime-boundary.md](docs/runtime-boundary.md) · [docs/operations.md](docs/operations.md) | | Native KVM, no QEMU | [docs/native-kvm-no-qemu.md](docs/native-kvm-no-qemu.md) | | Native macOS: the `vz` backend, sandboxes, container sandboxes, a Mac cloud | [docs/macos.md](docs/macos.md) · [docs/mac-cloud.md](docs/mac-cloud.md) · [docs/macos-sandboxes.md](docs/macos-sandboxes.md) · [docs/oci-sandboxes.md](docs/oci-sandboxes.md) | | Docker and Kubernetes on a Mac: `fluxctl docker`, `fluxctl kube` | [docs/docker-engine.md](docs/docker-engine.md) · [docs/kubernetes-on-mac.md](docs/kubernetes-on-mac.md) | | AI-agent sessions: install, quickstart, MCP, comparison | [docs/agent-platform/](docs/agent-platform/README.md) · [docs/agent-sessions.md](docs/agent-sessions.md) · [vs microsandbox](docs/vs-microsandbox.md) | | Agent sandboxes, procbox and the SDKs | [docs/agent-sandbox-gaps.md](docs/agent-sandbox-gaps.md) · [python/](python/README.md) · [go/](go/README.md) · [typescript/](typescript/README.md) | | Network Fabric and Service Fabric | [docs/network-fabric.md](docs/network-fabric.md) · [docs/service-fabric.md](docs/service-fabric.md) | | Secure Containers and MicroVM | [docs/secure-containers.md](docs/secure-containers.md) · [docs/microvm.md](docs/microvm.md) | | Production checklist and DevOps gates | [docs/PRODUCTION.md](docs/PRODUCTION.md) · [docs/DEVOPS.md](docs/DEVOPS.md) | | Architecture, FAQ and ecosystem | [docs/architecture.md](docs/architecture.md) · [docs/faq.md](docs/faq.md) · [docs/ecosystem.md](docs/ecosystem.md) | | Ranked backlog | [docs/NEXT-FEATURES.md](docs/NEXT-FEATURES.md) | ## Contributing & community - **Contributing:** build and test commands, PR expectations and repo layout, in [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md). - **Host hardening:** TOTP step-up for exec, a signed exec allow-list and signed rule packs, in [docs/host-hardening.md](docs/host-hardening.md). - **Security:** the current hardening bar and how to report a vulnerability, in [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md). - **Changelog:** [CHANGELOG.md](CHANGELOG.md). --- ## Maturity **Proof, not promises.** We only claim what has been run. Every line links to how it was verified. - **Kubernetes operator:** 9/9 checks on a real k3s cluster, including self-healing and no leaked QEMU. [Details](docs/proof-and-status.md) - **Multi-host fleet:** a central registry with load-aware placement across two physically separate hosts. [Details](docs/proof-and-status.md) - **Storage and networking:** qcow2/raw, LVM thin, NBD and Ceph RBD (against a real Rook cluster); NAT, TAP+bridge, netns+DHCP and macvtap, SSH-verified end to end. [Details](docs/proof-and-status.md) - **Bridge-less direct datapath:** measured −31% latency and +60% 64 B packet rate in the Pod case, on a veth stand-in with no real guest. [Method and data](docs/direct-datapath.md#-measured-forwarding-cost) - **Native KVM:** 2, 4 and 8-vCPU guests boot, pause and snapshot across every vCPU, and a real `fluxctl create` passes the agent and NoCloud gate. [Details](docs/native-kvm-no-qemu.md) - **The boundaries, up front:** multi-tenant controls are opt-in, not a public-cloud boundary, and boot numbers are a method, not a sizing SLA. [Read them](docs/proof-and-status.md) | Status | Areas | |---|---| | **GA** | Network Fabric (TC/eBPF, the default dataplane; nftables via explicit `mode = "legacy"`) · Secure Containers (containerd runtime-v2, not a Kata-equivalence claim) | | **Released (0.4.x)** | MCP server, agent sessions (`fluxctl agent`), `host_gpu` Metal/MLX inference, sandbox GPUs (Linux VFIO), enforced Kairon VM edge, VM-edge capture, VM fork, VM import, quiesced backups, fleet console | | **Built, not yet run on real hosts** | FluxMesh (overlay, DNS, relay, enrollment, public edge): unit tests only; see [Proof & status](docs/proof-and-status.md) | | **Not by design** | KubeVirt compatibility | --- ## Part of the Zyvor stack FluxVM is complete and useful on its own. **Certify with GuestKit → run and manage with FluxVM → convert/deploy with h2kvm.** | Product | Role next to FluxVM | |---|---| | **[Zyvor Fabric](https://github.com/zyvorai/zyvorai-fabric)** | Private cloud control plane on the same REST API — FluxVM runs the VMs, Fabric adds auth/RBAC, network policy and UX | | **[GuestKit](https://github.com/zyvorai/zyvor-guestkit)** | Offline disk scoring/repair; FluxVM's VM import uses it to repair the boot disk | | **[h2kvm](https://github.com/zyvorai/zyvor-h2kvm)** | Hypervisor → KVM convert + import; hands a certified disk to FluxVM to run | | **[Kairon](https://github.com/zyvorai/zyvor-kairon)** | Posts the VM-edge spec FluxVM enforces in its TC dataplane | → [zyvor.dev](https://zyvor.dev) --- ## Support Free under Apache-2.0. If it helps you, you can donate any amount you like: . A donation is voluntary and supports development and maintenance. It is not a purchase: it buys no support, SLA, features, priority or license, and it is not tax-deductible (Zyvor AI Labs Private Limited is a company, not a charity). Zyvor Enterprise (supported releases, SLAs, a named contact and enterprise features) is separate: [sales@zyvor.dev](mailto:sales@zyvor.dev). ## License and support FluxVM is **free and open source** under the [Apache License 2.0](LICENSE) — see [NOTICE](NOTICE). Copyright 2026 Zyvor AI Labs. The entire repository is under this one license; there is no dual-licensing or separately-licensed core component. **Zyvor Enterprise** adds what production teams ask for: supported releases, deployment and upgrade guidance, priority incident triage, a named technical contact and 24x7 critical intake. Plans and terms: [docs/SUBSCRIPTION-MODEL.md](docs/SUBSCRIPTION-MODEL.md) · [Pricing](https://zyvor.dev/pricing?utm_source=github&utm_medium=fluxvm&utm_campaign=readme_license) · [sales@zyvor.dev](mailto:sales@zyvor.dev). Report vulnerabilities per [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md). ---
### Put a real API in front of your VMs [![Book a demo](https://img.shields.io/badge/Book_a_demo-0071e3?style=for-the-badge)](https://zyvor.dev/schedule?utm_source=github&utm_medium=fluxvm&utm_campaign=readme_footer) [![30-day PoC](https://img.shields.io/badge/Start_a_30--day_PoC-000000?style=for-the-badge)](https://zyvor.dev/poc?utm_source=github&utm_medium=fluxvm&utm_campaign=readme_footer) [![Pricing](https://img.shields.io/badge/Pricing-1d1d1f?style=for-the-badge)](https://zyvor.dev/pricing?utm_source=github&utm_medium=fluxvm&utm_campaign=readme_footer) [![Contact sales](https://img.shields.io/badge/Contact_sales-2997ff?style=for-the-badge)](mailto:sales@zyvor.dev?subject=FluxVM) [![Star on GitHub](https://img.shields.io/github/stars/zyvorai/zyvor-fluxvm?style=for-the-badge&logo=github&label=Star&color=2997ff)](https://github.com/zyvorai/zyvor-fluxvm)
## Native macOS (Apple silicon) The daemon, API and `fluxctl` build and run natively on macOS, with a `vz` backend on Apple's Virtualization.framework for ARM64 Linux guests and, from a prepared template, macOS guests. See [docs/macos.md](docs/macos.md) for what is verified and what is not. ![Mac mini for home, Mac Studio for a team, MacBook Pro for development](docs/assets/macos/readme-macs.jpg) The same REST API and `fluxctl` now run on a [Mac mini](https://www.apple.com/in/mac-mini/) at home, a [Mac Studio](https://www.apple.com/in/mac-studio/) for a team or a [MacBook Pro](https://www.apple.com/in/macbook-pro/) on the road. Pair FluxVM with [Velora](https://github.com/zyvorai/zyvor-velora) (a private OpenAI-compatible LLM endpoint on MLX) and [Kairon](https://github.com/zyvorai/zyvor-kairon) (every Mac as a Kubernetes Node) and a few Macs become a quiet, low-power, on-premise inference cluster with real Linux VMs alongside. ![A private LLM cluster made of Macs](docs/assets/macos/readme-home-cluster.jpg) **Verified** on an Apple M4, macOS 27.2: Debian 13 through the API (create, SSH, pause, resume, stop, start, delete), plus port forwards, shared folders, named images, snapshots and warm starts, `fluxctl run`, [stacks](docs/macos-stacks.md) (`fluxctl up`), and [agent sandboxes](docs/macos-sandboxes.md) (a warm pool, offline and allow-listed network, speculate and changesets). [Container sandboxes](docs/oci-sandboxes.md) (an OCI image in its own VM, `fluxctl sandbox run`) pass `scripts/oci-live-test.sh` on the same hardware (exit codes, read-only root, exec, offline and allow-listed network, a private network, `linux/amd64` under Rosetta, a warm-pool claim); published TCP and UDP ports pass `scripts/oci-udp-ports-live-test.sh` (a datagram and a TCP line echoed by the container, a clash refused, delete frees the port); volumes, restart policies, health checks, `secret_env`, stacks, `--fleet` placement and the dashboard are unit-tested only. `scripts/vz-devices-live-test.sh` also passes (extra disks, USB hot-plug, console ports, Linux display size). macOS guests install from an IPSW, boot and clone on the same hardware by hand ([details](docs/macos.md#macos-guests)). On macOS 27, the custom Virtio device's control channel (ping, echo, stats, capabilities) works on a Debian 13 guest, `host-capabilities` reports the M4, and fleet placement for `vz` (the node heartbeat carries its Apple capabilities and `fluxvm-agent central` scores nodes with `apple_placement`) was checked on loopback with one real node plus fake nodes. **Not yet verified:** multi-Mac clusters on real hardware, Thunderbolt RDMA, macOS guests through the API, the shared vmnet broker and physical USB passthrough (both blocked on the test Mac by signing). Sizing, the cluster design (after GK Servis's [Mac Studio case study](https://www.gkservis.com/case-studies/llm-inference-cluster.html)) and the roadmap: [docs/macos-cluster.md](docs/macos-cluster.md).

👋 **Welcome** · [欢迎](docs/README-zh_cn.md "简体中文") · [歡迎](docs/README-zh_tw.md "繁體中文") · [ようこそ](docs/README-ja.md "日本語") · [환영합니다](docs/README-ko.md "한국어") · [Bienvenue](docs/README-fr.md "Français") · [Bienvenido](docs/README-es.md "Español") · [Bem-vindos](docs/README-pt-BR.md "Português (Brasil)") · [Willkommen](docs/README-de.md "Deutsch") · [Benvenuti](docs/README-it.md "Italiano") · [Bun venit](docs/README-ro.md "Română") · [أهلًا](docs/README-ar.md "العربية") · [Hoş geldiniz](docs/README-tr.md "Türkçe") · [Ласкаво просимо](docs/README-uk.md "Українська") · [Witamy](docs/README-pl.md "Polski") · [خوش آمدید](docs/README-fa.md "فارسی") · [Selamat datang](docs/README-id.md "Bahasa Indonesia") · [Chào mừng](docs/README-vi.md "Tiếng Việt") · [ยินดีต้อนรับ](docs/README-th.md "ไทย") · [Καλώς ήρθατε](docs/README-el.md "Ελληνικά") · [സ്വാഗതം](docs/README-ml.md "മലയാളം") # Flisk: your whole app, running on your computer with one command Describe an app to your AI helper, or type four commands yourself.
Flisk runs every part of it on your computer (the website, the back end, the database), connects them, and keeps them in sync as you change things. **Never written code? [Start here](docs/start/first-time.md)**, step by step, no experience needed · [Words you'll see](docs/start/words.md) [![Flisk Discord](https://img.shields.io/badge/Discord-Join%20Server-5865F2?logo=discord&logoColor=white)](https://discord.gg/Sjhb3tnq3) [![npm version](https://img.shields.io/npm/v/@flisk-sh/flisk.svg?style=flat&color=blue)](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@flisk-sh/flisk) [![npm weekly downloads](https://img.shields.io/npm/dw/@flisk-sh/flisk?style=flat&color=blue)](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@flisk-sh/flisk) [![GitHub stars](https://img.shields.io/github/stars/flisk-sh/flisk?style=flat&logo=github)](https://github.com/flisk-sh/flisk/stargazers) [![License: MIT](https://img.shields.io/badge/License-MIT-yellow.svg)](LICENSE)

Quick start · Why Flisk · Examples · Installation · FAQ · Documentation

[Website](https://flisk.sh/) · [Quickstart](https://flisk.sh/docs/quickstart/) · [Examples](https://flisk.sh/docs/examples/) · [Awesome Flisk](https://github.com/flisk-sh/awesome-flisk-framework) · [Demo](https://flisk-sh.github.io/flisk-demo-animation/) · [Report a bug](https://github.com/flisk-sh/flisk/issues) An illustrative Claude Code session in the Warp terminal. The Flisk commands, their output, and the URLs Flisk prints come from a real run. Copy the prompt from Try it.
## Is Flisk right for your team? Three quick questions; click the answer closest to your team. Not technical? Pick "not sure" where you need to. You get a score and a plain-English why.
1. What is the app written in?
2. How do developers start the app on their laptop today?
3. How many parts does the app have? (website, API, background jobs, …)

**Great fit.** Flisk was made for teams like yours. [Why this score →](docs/fit/node-compose-5-plus.md) · [Full calculator on flisk.sh](https://flisk.sh/fit/) ## Trusted by

Teams that run flisk up on their own code, listed with their consent. See all adopters or add yours.

## Try it ### With your AI agent Install Flisk, then paste a prompt into your [AI helper](docs/start/words.md#ai-helper): Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, or any other that can run commands. Every grey box below has a copy button: paste the first one into your [terminal](docs/start/words.md#terminal), and the prompt into your helper. ```bash npm install -g @flisk-sh/flisk ``` **The prompt from the demo:** ```text Build me a small online shop with a storefront and an orders API, and run it on my laptop with Flisk. ``` Your helper creates the project, adds each part of the app, and starts it. Then open the link Flisk prints, like `http://localhost:3000`, in your browser: that is your app, on your computer. If something is missing, `flisk doctor` says what, in plain words.
More prompts to copy **Add a service to a project you already have** ```text Use Flisk to add a backend service called payments-api to my shop stack, then start the stack and give me the URLs. ``` **Build an AI agent with tools and a database** ```text Use Flisk to scaffold an AI agent, an MCP tools server, and a database in one stack called shop, then start it and tell me how to talk to the agent. ``` **Something is not working** ```text Run flisk doctor, explain every problem in plain words, and fix what you can. Then start my stack with flisk up. ``` **See what is running** ```text Use flisk status to tell me which services are running, which are unhealthy, and what URL each one has. ``` **Stop everything** ```text Stop my Flisk stack with flisk down and confirm nothing is left running. ```
#### Pick your agent Each AI helper installs a little differently; pick yours for the exact steps. After that it is the same everywhere: paste the prompt, and the helper runs Flisk for you. (For developers: `flisk project` also adds the Flisk skills and an `AGENTS.md` to your project, so the agent knows how to use Flisk.)
```bash curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.sh | bash npm install -g @flisk-sh/flisk ``` Then start Claude Code by typing `claude` in your project folder, and paste the prompt above. For developers: `flisk project` writes the Flisk skills to `.claude/skills/`, which Claude Code loads. To let Claude Code drive Flisk through MCP tools, run `claude mcp add --scope project flisk -- flisk mcp`. Windows install, the `.mcp.json` file and the `AGENTS.md` tip: [full Claude Code setup](docs/agents/claude-code.md).
Any other agent that can run terminal commands works too. Point it at `AGENTS.md`, or connect it to `flisk mcp`, which runs an MCP server over stdio. ### In your terminal

```bash npm install -g @flisk-sh/flisk mkdir my-shop && cd my-shop flisk project --yes flisk resource orders-api --type backend --stack shop --yes flisk resource shop-web --type frontend --stack shop --yes flisk up shop ``` You get a working shop on your computer: a storefront website and an orders back end, with a [database](docs/start/words.md#database), one address to open, and changes that show up as you save. In developer terms: an orders API and a storefront behind one local gateway, with Postgres and live reload. You need [Docker](docs/start/words.md#docker), [Tilt](https://docs.tilt.dev/install.html), Node.js 22.12+, and [Bun](https://bun.sh/) 1.2+; `flisk doctor` checks your machine. A simpler app needs none of those: give each service a `command` and [run it as local processes](docs/run-without-docker.md). Prefer to answer questions instead? `npm init create-microservices my-project` asks what to create. See the [quick start](#quick-start) for every option.

### Your AI helper writes the app. Flisk handles the plumbing. AI helpers are great at writing the app itself, and bad at the setup around it: the files that start each part, connect the parts and give them a database. Every time an AI rewrites that setup by hand, something breaks, and you pay for the time and the AI tokens it takes to fix. (For developers: a rewritten `Dockerfile`, a misconfigured `Tiltfile`, a broken `nginx.conf`.) **Flisk** writes that setup for you, the same way every time, and keeps it in sync. Docker Compose and Tilt are tools developers use to start the parts of an app on their computer. Compose runs [containers](docs/start/words.md#container) from a YAML settings file you write. [Tilt](docs/start/words.md#tilt) watches your files and live-updates the running app as you save them, from a Tiltfile you write. Flisk writes both files for you from one small `service.json` per service (per part of your app), then runs Tilt. | | Docker Compose | Tilt | Flisk | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Scaffold a new service in one command | Partial (`docker init` writes a Dockerfile and compose file) | No | Yes (`flisk resource`) | | Hot reload on file change | Partial (`compose watch`) | Yes (`live_update`) | Yes (generated Tilt `live_update`) | | Health-checked startup order | Yes (`depends_on: condition: service_healthy`) | Yes (`resource_deps`, written by hand) | Yes (from `dependsOn`) | | Gateway URL per service and Postgres included | No (you add them) | No (you add them) | Yes (Traefik `*.localhost` and Postgres) | | Start one stack of a large system | Partial (profiles) | Yes (`tilt up `) | Yes (`flisk up `) | | Config you write by hand | `compose.yaml` | `Tiltfile` (Starlark) | `service.json` only; the rest is generated and drift-checked | **Where they are stronger** - **Compose** is the simpler choice for two or three services you already containerized, and it needs no Tilt. - **Tilt** gives full control when you are happy to write and maintain a Tiltfile, and it also targets Kubernetes. **Use them together.** Flisk generates a Compose file and a Tiltfile and runs them with Docker and Tilt, so the generated files stay readable with `flisk config explain`. --- ### Pick how to start Four ways to get your app running: the simplest one, a one-command demo, a project you set up by hand, and a guided setup that asks you questions. The simplest is below; each tab opens its own page.
Run your app on your own computer with one command, without Docker. This path fits an app made of a few [parts](docs/start/words.md#app-parts) that each start with one [command](docs/start/words.md#command), for example a back end (an API), a website and a worker. You need only Flisk and the program that runs your code, such as [Node.js](docs/start/words.md#nodejs). **For developers:** each service runs as a local process. You need only Flisk and your app's runtime. **1. Install Flisk.** Paste this into your [terminal](docs/start/words.md#terminal) and press Enter: ```bash npm install -g @flisk-sh/flisk ``` **2. Describe each part.** Put a small settings file called `service.json` in each part's folder (next to each service). It tells Flisk the part's name, the command that starts it and the [port](docs/start/words.md#port) it listens on. This one is for the back end: ```json { "schemaVersion": 1, "appName": "api", "appType": "backend", "command": "node server.js", "port": 4000, "healthCheckPath": "/health" } ``` This one is for the website. `"dependsOn": ["api"]` means "start the back end first": ```json { "schemaVersion": 1, "appName": "web", "appType": "frontend", "command": "node server.js", "port": 3000, "dependsOn": ["api"] } ``` **3. Start everything.** In the terminal, go to your project folder and run: ```bash flisk up ``` What you will see: Flisk starts the API, waits until it answers, then starts the website. It prints both URLs (the web addresses to open in your browser; they are [localhost](docs/start/words.md#localhost) links, so only you can see them). Each line of output starts with the name of the part that wrote it. If a part crashes, Flisk starts it again. To stop, press Ctrl+C (hold Control and press C), or run `flisk down`. No Docker, no Tilt, no generated files. See [Run your app without Docker](docs/run-without-docker.md) for every field, and for when to switch to the full stack with a [database](docs/start/words.md#database) and one gateway URL (one web address for every part).

For the two-service shop above, Flisk writes the rest at three levels: the project, the stack, and each service. ```text my-shop/ ├── .env # generated DB_PASSWORD and JWT_SECRET ├── .flisk/ │ ├── project.json # project settings (yours to edit) │ └── .flisk-out/ # PROJECT LEVEL │ ├── Tiltfile # what Tilt runs │ ├── docker-compose.traefik.yml # local gateway, bound to 127.0.0.1 │ ├── golden-layers.Dockerfile # shared base image layers │ ├── TILT_TECH_STACK.star # tech stack settings │ ├── TILT_RESOURCE_DEFAULTS.star # service defaults │ ├── spec.master # project spec by stack │ └── flisk-cli-ext/ # pinned copy of the Flisk engine ├── shared-platform-engineering/ │ └── docker-templates/ # container entrypoint scripts └── services/ ├── platform/database-management/ │ └── docker-compose.yml # Postgres 16 └── shop/ ├── .autogenerated/ # STACK LEVEL │ └── docker-compose.app.autogenerated.yml # every service in the stack ├── orders-api/ │ ├── service.json # you write this │ └── .autogenerated/ # SERVICE LEVEL: 14 files └── shop-web/ ├── service.json # you write this └── .autogenerated/ # SERVICE LEVEL: 18 files ``` The stack's Compose file is the part you would otherwise write by hand. For these two services it holds the image builds, environment, 33 Traefik routing labels, four networks, health checks, and CPU and memory limits. An excerpt: ```yaml orders-api: environment: - DATABASE_URL=postgresql://my_shop:${DB_PASSWORD}@my_shop_postgres:5432/my_shop_shop?schema=public - JWT_SECRET=${JWT_SECRET:?JWT_SECRET is not set. Run `flisk up` ...} labels: - "traefik.http.routers.orders-api-project.rule=Host(`api.my-shop.localhost`) && PathPrefix(`/api/orders`)" - "traefik.http.middlewares.orders-api-strip-prefix-project.stripprefix.prefixes=/api/orders" - "traefik.http.services.orders-api.loadbalancer.healthcheck.path=/health" healthcheck: test: ["CMD", "curl", "-f", "--max-time", "5", "http://localhost:4000/health"] ``` Secrets come from the project `.env` by default: `flisk project` generates a random database password and JWT secret, and `.env` is added to `.gitignore`. Tilt's projection of service.json ├── validation-report.autogenerated.json # preflight validation result ├── AGENTS.md # tells coding agents not to edit here └── .flisk-contract/ # snapshots for drift checks ``` ```text orders-api/.autogenerated/ ├── Dockerfile.app.autogenerated # app image ├── Dockerfile.app.autogenerated.dockerignore # build context ├── vite.config.backend.autogenerated.ts # server build ├── prisma.config.autogenerated.ts # database client ├── tsconfig.autogenerated.json # Bun 1.2+ is used by the default generated services. Flisk selects host ports from bounded fallback ranges for HTTP, HTTPS, and Postgres; set `FLISK_HTTP_PORT`, `FLISK_HTTPS_PORT`, or `FLISK_POSTGRES_PORT` to override them. Dev ports listen on `127.0.0.1` only, so other machines on your network cannot reach them. Set `FLISK_BIND_ADDRESS` (for example `0.0.0.0`, to test from a phone) to change that; `flisk doctor` warns when it is a wildcard address. Flisk supports macOS, Linux, and **Windows through WSL2 Ubuntu**; native Windows supports CLI inspection only (`flisk --version`, `flisk doctor`, `flisk up --dry-run`). `flisk up` exits with a clear refusal pointing to WSL2. See the **[Windows & WSL2 guide](docs/wsl2.md)** for the recommended setup, prerequisites, verification steps, and troubleshooting. On native Windows, `flisk --version`, `flisk doctor`, and `flisk up --dry-run` are inspect-only commands. `flisk up` exits 1 with “Landscape startup needs Ubuntu on WSL2. Native Windows is inspect-only.” ## License matrix | Capability | Free | Premium | | --- | --- | --- | | `flisk up`, scaffold, Traefik, Postgres, Tilt live update, golden layers | yes | yes | | Verdaccio, DDD scaffold, Sablier idle stop | no | key | | Playwright, C4, AGENTS.md | free if generated in-repo | only if the implementation is downloaded with a key | Core stays free. Premium is a separate key for the extras above; no key required to run `flisk up`. **Ecosystem map:** examples, articles, related tools, and notes live in [awesome-flisk-framework](https://github.com/flisk-sh/awesome-flisk-framework). ## FAQ
I have never written code. Is Flisk for me? Yes, if you build with an AI helper like Claude Code, Codex or Cursor. You describe the app; the helper writes it and uses Flisk to run it on your computer. [Start here](docs/start/first-time.md) walks you through it step by step, and [Words you'll see](docs/start/words.md) explains the terms. You will paste a few commands into a terminal, but you do not need to write any code.
Does it cost anything? The Flisk command-line tool is free and open source (MIT); optional Premium extras need a key (see the [license matrix](#license-matrix)). Your AI helper has its own plans and prices. Bigger apps also use Docker Desktop, which is free for personal use and small companies.
Do I need Kubernetes? No. Flisk runs your services with Docker and Tilt on your machine. It does not need a local cluster such as kind or minikube, and it does not replace Helm, Compose, or your production deployment tools.
Do I need a license key? No. Core CLI is MIT and needs no key to run `flisk up`. Premium extras are optional and use a separate key (see the [license matrix](#license-matrix)).
Which platforms are supported? macOS and Linux are supported directly. Windows is supported through WSL2 Ubuntu; native Windows supports CLI inspection only (`flisk --version`, `flisk doctor`, `flisk up --dry-run`). See [Requirements and support](#requirements-and-support) and the **[Windows & WSL2 guide](docs/wsl2.md)** for the recommended setup, prerequisites, verification steps, and troubleshooting.
Does Flisk send my code anywhere? Flisk runs the local stack on your machine. For network calls, secrets, and supply-chain details, see [security: network calls, secrets and supply chain](docs/security.md).
Can I keep using Compose, Helm, or my own Tilt setup? Yes. If your existing setup already gives you a working local environment, keep using it. See [working alongside Helm](docs/with-helm.md) and [gradual adoption](docs/gradual-adoption.md) for adding Flisk to an existing repository.
What should I do if I hit a bug? Update first; a recent release may already fix it. Run `flisk upgrade` (also available as `flisk update`), or: ```bash npm install -g @flisk-sh/flisk@latest ``` Then run `flisk doctor` and retry the same task. If the problem persists, [open an issue](https://github.com/flisk-sh/flisk/issues) with your Flisk version, operating system, steps to reproduce, and the error output. See [upgrading and version pinning](docs/upgrading.md) and [troubleshooting](docs/troubleshooting.md).
## Contributing and license Contributions are welcome. **First step: [say hello on Discord](https://discord.gg/Sjhb3tnq3)**, tell us what you want to work on, and we will point you to a good first task. Then start with [CONTRIBUTING.md](.github/CONTRIBUTING.md) and the [contributor guide](docs/contributing/README.md). For the project structure, see the [architecture and repository map](docs/project-overview.md). To review pull requests, see [Review a pull request](docs/contributing/04-review-a-pr.md). Report security issues using [SECURITY.md](.github/SECURITY.md). ### Contributors Thank you to everyone who has shipped code, docs, and fixes to Flisk since July 2026. Every merged change makes the local stack better for the next developer.

items.readme_text: # llama3pure Three inference engines for Llama 3: pure C for desktop systems, pure JavaScript for Node.js, and pure JavaScript for Web environments. Supports both Llama and Gemma architectures. Try the Web engine [here](https://lrusso.github.io/llama3pure/llama3pure-web-demo.htm). ![demo](https://github.com/lrusso/llama3pure/blob/main/README.gif?raw=true) ## Table of Contents - [Building the engine (macOS / Linux)](#building-the-engine-macos--linux) - [Building the engine (Windows)](#building-the-engine-windows) - [Running the engine (macOS / Linux / Windows)](#running-the-engine-macos--linux--windows) - [Running in Node.js](#running-in-nodejs) - [Running in Web Environments](#running-in-web-environments) - [Suggested Models and Engines](#suggested-models-and-engines) - [Tested Models](#tested-models) - [Special Keys](#special-keys) - [Author's Notes](#authors-notes) - [Credits](#based-on-the-work-of) ## Building the engine (macOS / Linux) ```bash make llama3pure ``` ## Building the engine (Windows) Use the x64 Native Tools Command Prompt for VS. ```bash cl /O2 llama3pure-c-engine.c /Fe:llama3pure.exe ``` ## Running the engine (macOS / Linux / Windows) ```bash # On macOS / Linux ./llama3pure -model Llama3.gguf -prompt "Tell me in 1 line what is Microsoft." ./llama3pure -model Llama3.gguf -chathistory chat.txt # On Windows llama3pure.exe -model Llama3.gguf -prompt "Tell me in 1 line what is Microsoft." llama3pure.exe -model Llama3.gguf -chathistory chat.txt ``` | Argument | Required | Description | Default Value | | :------------- | :------: | :------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | :----------------------------: | | -model | Yes | Path to a GGUF model file. | - | | -prompt | No | Input prompt text (single-turn, alternative to -chathistory). | - | | -chathistory | No | Path to a .txt file containing a JSON chat history (multi-turn, alternative to -prompt). | - | | -system_prompt | No | System prompt prepended to every conversation. | `You are a helpful assistant.` | | -max_tokens | No | Maximum number of tokens to generate per response. | -1 (unlimited) | | -context_size | No | Context window size (capped by the model's own limit). | Model's max. | | -temperature | No | Sampling temperature. Higher values produce more varied output. | 0.9 | | -top_p | No | Nucleus sampling threshold. Only tokens whose cumulative probability reaches this value are considered. | 0.9 | | -top_k | No | Top-K sampling. Only the K most probable tokens are considered at each step. | 40 | | -debug | No | Show detailed model loading and performance logs (including tok/s). | disabled | Sample chat history in [tests.txt](https://github.com/lrusso/llama3pure/blob/main/tests.txt). A message with `"type": "system"` sets the system prompt, taking precedence over `-system_prompt`. ## Running in Node.js - Step 1: Load a model Read the GGUF file into an ArrayBuffer and pass it to `llama3pure` with `type: "load"`. ```javascript import llama3pure from "./llama3pure-js-engine.js" import fs from "fs" const readFileAsArrayBuffer = (filePath) => { const fd = fs.openSync(filePath, "r") const fileSize = fs.fstatSync(fd).size const arrayBuffer = new ArrayBuffer(fileSize) const fileUint8 = new Uint8Array(arrayBuffer) const chunkSize = 256 * 1024 * 1024 let pos = 0 while (pos < fileSize) { const toRead = Math.min(chunkSize, fileSize - pos) fs.readSync(fd, fileUint8, pos, toRead, pos) pos = pos + toRead } fs.closeSync(fd) return arrayBuffer } llama3pure({ type: "load", model: readFileAsArrayBuffer("/path/to/your-model.gguf"), cbRender: (token) => { process.stdout.write(token) }, systemPrompt: "You are a helpful assistant.", maxTokens: 256, contextSize: 2048, temperature: 0.9, topP: 0.9, topK: 40, }) ``` | Parameter | Type | Required | Description | Default Value | | :----------- | :---------: | :------: | :------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | :----------------------------: | | type | string | Yes | Must be `load` | - | | model | ArrayBuffer | Yes | The GGUF model file contents. | - | | cbRender | function | Yes | Callback invoked with each generated token as a string. | - | | systemPrompt | string | No | System prompt prepended to every conversation. | `You are a helpful assistant.` | | maxTokens | number | No | Maximum number of tokens to generate per response. | -1 (unlimited) | | contextSize | number | No | Context window size (capped by the model's own limit). | Model's max. | | temperature | number | No | Sampling temperature. Higher values produce more varied output. | 0.9 | | topP | number | No | Nucleus sampling threshold. Only tokens whose cumulative probability reaches this value are considered. | 0.9 | | topK | number | No | Top-K sampling. Only the K most probable tokens are considered at each step. | 40 | - Step 2: Generate a response Call `llama3pure` with `type: "generate"` and a `chatHistory` array. The engine uses the `cbRender` callback provided during load to stream tokens. The last message in `chatHistory` should have `type: "user"` - that is the message the model will respond to. Previous messages provide conversation context, enabling multi-turn conversations. A message with `type: "system"` sets the system prompt, taking precedence over `systemPrompt`. ```javascript llama3pure({ type: "generate", chatHistory: [ { type: "user", text: "Tell me in 1 line what is Microsoft." }, { type: "model", response: [ "Microsoft is a global technology leader known for its innovative products and services.", ], }, { type: "user", text: "Tell me in 1 line the names of the founders." }, ], }) ``` | Parameter | Type | Required | Description | | :---------- | :----: | :------: | :------------------------------------------------------ | | type | string | Yes | Must be `generate`. | | chatHistory | array | Yes | Array of message objects representing the conversation. | Full example in [llama3pure-nodejs-demo.js](https://github.com/lrusso/llama3pure/blob/main/llama3pure-nodejs-demo.js). ## Running in Web Environments - Step 1: Load a model Read the GGUF file as an ArrayBuffer and send it to the worker with type: "load". The ArrayBuffer is transferred (not copied) for performance. ```javascript const reader = new FileReader() reader.onload = (event) => { const arrayBuffer = event.target.result worker.postMessage( { type: "load", model: arrayBuffer, systemPrompt: "You are a helpful assistant.", maxTokens: 256, contextSize: 2048, temperature: 0.9, topP: 0.9, topK: 40, }, [arrayBuffer] ) } reader.readAsArrayBuffer(file) ``` | Parameter | Type | Required | Description | Default Value | | :----------- | :---------: | :------: | :------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | :----------------------------: | | type | string | Yes | Must be `load` | - | | model | ArrayBuffer | Yes | The GGUF model file contents. | - | | systemPrompt | string | No | System prompt prepended to every conversation. | `You are a helpful assistant.` | | maxTokens | number | No | Maximum number of tokens to generate per response. | -1 (unlimited) | | contextSize | number | No | Context window size (capped by the model's own limit). | Model's max. | | temperature | number | No | Sampling temperature. Higher values produce more varied output. | 0.9 | | topP | number | No | Nucleus sampling threshold. Only tokens whose cumulative probability reaches this value are considered. | 0.9 | | topK | number | No | Top-K sampling. Only the K most probable tokens are considered at each step. | 40 | - Step 2: Generate a response ```javascript worker.postMessage({ type: "generate", chatHistory: [ { type: "user", text: "Tell me in 1 line what is Microsoft." }, { type: "model", response: [ "Microsoft is a global technology leader known for its innovative products and services.", ], }, { type: "user", text: "Tell me in 1 line the names of the founders." }, ], }) ``` | Parameter | Type | Required | Description | | :---------- | :----: | :------: | :------------------------------------------------------ | | type | string | Yes | Must be `generate`. | | chatHistory | array | Yes | Array of message objects representing the conversation. | - Step 3: Receiving messages from the Worker ```javascript worker.onmessage = function (e) { var data = e.data switch (data.type) { case "progress": // Fired during model loading break case "loaded": // Fired once the model is fully loaded and ready break case "token": // Fired for each generated token during inference console.log(data.token) break case "complete": // Fired when generation is finished console.log(data.output) break } } ``` | Event | Fields | Description | | :------- | :-------------: | :--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | progress | - | Emitted during model loading to indicate progress. | | loaded | - | Emitted once when the model has been fully loaded and is ready for inference. | | token | token (string) | Emitted for each token as it is generated, enabling real-time streaming of the response. | | complete | output (string) | Emitted when generation finishes. Contains the full generated text. | Try the Web engine [here](https://lrusso.github.io/llama3pure/llama3pure-web-demo.htm) or with custom `maxTokens`, `contextSize`, `topP` and `topK` [here](https://lrusso.github.io/llama3pure/llama3pure-web-demo.htm?maxTokens=2048&contextSize=4096&topP=0.9&topK=40). A standalone version is available [here](https://lrusso.github.io/llama3pure/llama3pure-web-standalone.htm); it offers the same functionality as the standard version but uses a base64-embedded Worker, allowing you to run it as a local file without a web server. ## Suggested Models and Engines | MODEL | C | NODE.JS | WEB | | [Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct-Q8_0.gguf](https://huggingface.co/bartowski/Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct-GGUF/resolve/main/Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct-Q8_0.gguf?download=true) | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | | items.title: OpenAI 宣布 AI 模型取得三项科学突破，涉及局部光滑猜想、指数时间假设与杨–米尔斯理论
items.summary: OpenAI 于 10 月 27 日宣布其 AI 模型在数学、计算机科学和物理学领域取得三项研究突破。数学上给出了所有维度下局部光滑猜想的证明，从而解决挂谷猜想与斯坦因限制猜想；计算机科学上给出推翻指数时间假设（ETH）的证明，暗示相关计算任务可能有更快算法；物理学上提出量子色动力学及标准模型一种统一完备化的严格存在性证明，涉及杨–米尔斯千禧年难题的一部分。
items.original_text: 感谢IT之家网友 Stephen_233 、 乌蝇哥的左手 、 补药吖 的线索投递！ IT之家 10 月 27 日消息，OpenAI 宣布，其 AI 模型在数学、计算机科学和物理学领域取得三项重大突破，展现出 AI 独立发现并证明复杂科学理论的能力，而不只是回答问题或辅助研究。 在数学领域，AI 证明了适用于所有维度的局部光滑猜想，并由此解决 局部光滑猜想与挂谷猜想 。 在计算机科学领域，AI 推翻了 长期被广泛接受的指数时间假设 ，意味着未来可能找到速度更快的算法。 在物理学领域，AI 提出 量子色动力学及杨–米尔斯理论的严格数学存在性证明 ，涉及世界七大千禧年数学难题之一。 OpenAI 表示，数学和计算机科学成果已通过 Lean 数学验证工具进行形式化验证，并公开证明材料；物理学成果正由诺贝尔物理学奖得主等专家参与审查。相关成果仍需学术界进一步独立确认。 IT之家附上 OpenAI 官方的声明大意如下： 局部光滑猜想与挂谷猜想 数学方面的新成果来自调和分析领域。 1991 年，数学家克里斯托弗 · 索格提出局部光滑猜想，试图解释波在聚焦时的行为。按照该猜想，波即使出现极其强烈的聚焦，也只能持续很短的时间。如果随机选取一个具有代表性的时刻，观察到的聚焦程度总会远低于最极端的情况。 数学中经常出现类似现象：某种现象在最坏情况下可以达到非常极端的程度，但经过平均处理后，实际观察到的情况要温和得多。 局部光滑猜想描述的现象具有基础性意义，因此涉及数学分析的众多问题。其中，挂谷猜想和斯坦因限制猜想都可以由局部光滑猜想推导出来。 2019 年，古思、王虹和张睿翔证明了二维空间中的局部光滑猜想。2025 年，王虹与扎尔又证明了三维挂谷猜想。 OpenAI 的模型此次给出了局部光滑猜想在所有维度下的证明，从而也解决了所有维度下的挂谷猜想和斯坦因限制猜想。证明的关键是一种新构建的辅助偏微分方程。 OpenAI 于 2026 年 10 月 18 日获得 AI 生成的证明，并在第二天完成 Lean 形式化证明。随后，OpenAI 联系外部专家，讨论如何围绕该成果建立合作机制。 根据专家建议，OpenAI 决定直接公开 AI 生成的证明，采用与 10 月 6 日发布研究成果时相同的方式。目前，模型撰写的自然语言证明和 Lean 形式化证明均已上传至公开的 GitHub 代码仓库。 指数时间假设被推翻 计算机科学方面的发现涉及指数时间假设（ETH）。 ETH 是计算复杂性理论中一个存在已久的猜想，研究布尔公式可满足性问题的计算难度，与著名的 P 和 NP 问题密切相关。 长期以来，学术界 普遍认为 ETH 成立 。数百篇研究论文以该假设为前提，推导出图论、计算生物学、数据库和计算几何等领域的计算难度结论。 近期，OpenAI 的系统却 给出了 ETH 不成立的证明 ，并通过 Lean 完成了形式化验证。 ETH 被推翻后，研究人员需要重新审视许多计算任务 究竟还能获得多大幅度的速度提升 。新成果也有助于指导更高效算法的研究。不过，要找到能够实现这些提升的算法，并将理论成果转化为实际应用，仍需要大量后续研究。 OpenAI 邀请三位算法设计和计算复杂性理论专家牵头，负责验证、研究和解释这项成果，分别是加利福尼亚大学圣迭戈分校的拉塞尔 · 因帕利亚佐和拉马莫汉 · 帕图里，以及麻省理工学院的瑞安 · 威廉姆斯。 三位专家在该领域都有长期研究积累： OpenAI 接受了合作团队提出的两项要求：首先，公开研究成果的所有原始数据，方便其他研究人员独立验证；其次，由 OpenAI 提供资金，举办一场学术会议，讨论新成果对计算机科学领域的整体影响。 合作团队还邀请学术界共同组织对 ETH 证明的公开审查，并就 AI 研究突破引发的问题展开讨论，包括如何验证成果、如何开放研究资料、如何认定学术贡献，以及未来应如何开展科研工作。 OpenAI 于 10 月 16 日生成了推翻 ETH 的自然语言证明，10 月 17 日又完成了 Lean 形式化证明。随后，OpenAI 开始着手建立前述外部合作机制。 模型生成的自然语言证明 和 Lean 证明 现已在 OpenAI 的公开 GitHub 代码仓库发布。 量子色动力学的存在性与标准模型的统一完备化 物理学方面，OpenAI 提出了一项关于量子场论存在性的研究成果。 该成果从严格的数学意义上，证明了四维空间中某些 包含规范场和费米子的相互作用量子场论确实存在 ，其中包括量子色动力学（QCD），以及粒子物理学标准模型的一种统一完备化理论。 证明采用了构造性量子场论中巴拉班提出的研究方法。此外，研究还解决了一个子问题，即证明纯杨-米尔斯理论的存在性。该问题属于克雷数学研究所设立的量子杨-米尔斯理论千禧年大奖难题的一部分。 粒子物理学标准模型描述了亚原子基本粒子之间的相互作用，涵盖自然界四种基本相互作用中的三种，不包括引力。 由于标准模型本身无法直接推广至任意短的距离尺度，OpenAI 的存在性证明针对的是 包含标准模型规范场和费米子的最简单大统一理论 。 量子色动力学研究夸克、胶子等粒子如何通过强相互作用发生联系。纯杨-米尔斯理论研究的范围更窄，只涉及传递强相互作用的胶子之间的自相互作用，不包括夸克等物质粒子。 OpenAI 邀请大卫 · 格罗斯牵头研究，团队其他成员包括迈克尔 · 道格拉斯、阿瑟 · 贾菲、伊戈尔 · 克莱巴诺夫和尼基塔 · 涅克拉索夫。 五位学者在量子场论及数学物理领域均有重要贡献： 大卫 · 格罗斯： 1973 年，他参与的杨-米尔斯理论渐近自由研究，为量子色动力学成为公认的强相互作用理论奠定了基础，并使他获得 2004 年诺贝尔物理学奖。渐近自由也是严格证明这些理论在数学上存在的关键机制。 阿瑟 · 贾菲：他与威滕共同制定了量子杨-米尔斯理论千禧年大奖难题，也是千禧年大奖难题设立构想的提出者之一，并参与创办克雷数学研究所。 迈克尔 · 道格拉斯：过去 20 年，他一直参与推动该问题的研究，曾于 2004 年报告研究进展，并在今年年初全面梳理了最新成果。 伊戈尔 · 克莱巴诺夫：他较早将规范场与弦理论的对偶性用于研究禁闭现象，这是量子色动力学的重要性质。他目前负责西蒙斯基金会的禁闭与量子色动力学弦合作研究项目。 尼基塔 · 涅克拉索夫：他在杨-米尔斯理论推广形式的精确求解方法方面取得了开创性成果，并于 2023 年获得丹尼 · 海涅曼数学物理奖。 参考 广告声明：文内含有的对外跳转链接（包括不限于超链接、二维码、口令等形式），用于传递更多信息，节省甄选时间，结果仅供参考，IT之家包含外链的文章均包含本声明。

items.title: Gamma 发布 Gamma 5 及 credits、导出、预览等多项更新
items.summary: Gamma 发布 Gamma 5，宣称重建了思考、设计和编辑方式，支持输入句子、文档、PDF、图片或旧演示文稿，由智能体在几分钟内完成调研和设计，并可连接 Slack、Notion、Granola 等 20+ 工具引入上下文。
items.original_text: Introducing Gamma 5 We rebuilt how Gamma thinks, designs, and edits. Because your best ideas deserve better. Give Gamma 5 whatever you have: a sentence, a doc, a PDF, an image, an old deck. The agent will then brainstorm, research, and design a polished presentation within minutes. Bring in PDF and PPT designs for ongoing use. Edit however you'd like, then export - your changes stay intact. Skip the copy-and-paste. Connect Slack, Notion, Granola, and 20+ other tools to bring in context directly. Gamma builds the story around your data. Describe the look you want, or share visual inspiration. Gamma tailors a style to your goal, so the result is specific to your content, not generic. Clearer credit balances Check your balance more easily from your home screen and Billing settings, with clearer credit information and an out-of-credits state. Learn how credits work. Exports that stay closer to your design PowerPoint exports better preserve custom fonts in multilingual text, equations, and table emoji and layouts. Tall charts in classic Gammas also fit PowerPoint and Google Slides more reliably when Scale to fit is enabled. Explore export options. Previews that match your format New and updated Gammas now show previews that better reflect their format, including portrait documents, social posts, and 4:3 slides. Older previews refresh after you edit the Gamma, making your work easier to recognize across your library and templates.

items.title: Anthropic S-1 文件中的五个不寻常细节
items.summary: The Verge 梳理 Anthropic 向 SEC 提交的 300 多页 S-1 上市文件，列出五个细节。
items.original_text: Anthropic has finally filed its S-1 prospectus with the SEC, a document designed to give investors a look under the hood of its business, from how much its executives are making and plans for spending its IPO billions to the risks that could derail its ambitions. At more than 300 pages, there’s a lot to unpack, and some of the disclosures have not previously been reported. Here are some of the biggest things that jumped out to us from our first pass: Sibling co-founders Dario Amodei and Daniela Amodei are the two most highly-paid executives at Anthropic, according to the filing. Last year, CEO Dario’s compensation totaled nearly $18 million, most of which came from stock and option awards. President Daniela, meanwhile, received $16.4 million. Admittedly, it is at the lower end of the Big Tech scale , but it is still a tidy sum. And that’s not all. Anthropic also spent $2.75 million on “personal security services” for Dario and $1.29 million for “personal protection, home security, and transportation services” for Daniela. Dario also gets access to a private jet for personal use, which cost the company another $97,055. The company says its success is “highly dependent on the continued service” of its senior team, particularly Dario and Daniela, who “are critical” to advancing the company’s research and mission. Anthropic has some pretty existential risk factors Every S-1 features a long list of things that could go wrong. Anthropic’s is no exception. But alongside standard warnings about competition, regulation, and market shifts, there are some less conventional risks too. For one, Anthropic warns that AI systems could cause potentially “catastrophic” harm, potentially of a kind that could not be underwritten by the entire “insurance industry in the aggregate.” As AI systems become more sophisticated, there’s also the question of whether Claude — or any other AI system — could possess or develop “forms of sentience.” Such a scenario would present some rather unusual business challenges. There’s also the possibility they “may behave in unintended, misaligned, or autonomous ways” that could damage the company. It’s no secret that Anthropic needs compute, but the sheer scale of its spending is staggering. The filing details billions of dollars of commitments to secure the compute needed to power its AI models, including roughly $3.1 billion per month to SpaceX for access to Nvidia GPUs once all of the planned capacity is delivered, totaling as much as $120.5 billion by 2029. Other commitments include spending $44.9 billion with Microsoft through 2033, at least $114.5 billion with Google through 2033, and $110 billion with Amazon over the next ten years. Anthropic also plans to expand its own “infrastructure footprint,” including overseas, as it faces increasing opposition to data center development in the US. It has a really weird corporate structure Anthropic already has a somewhat complicated corporate structure as a public benefit corporation. But there’s another unusual twist that will allow its seven cofounders to retain considerable control over the company even after it goes public. Through a separate corporate entity called “Founder LLC,” the group will collectively control 50.1 percent of shareholder voting power over key matters. Anthropic says the seven founders “are distinctly equipped to be stewards of our mission” of benefiting humanity through responsible AI development. Anthropic names only two rivals There’s no shortage of AI models out there, but when it comes to “direct competition,” Anthropic names just two other developers: OpenAI and Google. Condolences to SpaceX, Meta, and the rest of the AI world. Follow topics and authors from this story to see more like this in your personalized homepage feed and to receive email updates. Robert Hart
