items.title: Artificial Analysis 评测 GPT-6.1 Terra：以不到三分之一成本推进性价比前沿
items.source: Artificial Analysis 完整文章（网页）
items.summary: Artificial Analysis 评测 OpenAI 发布的 GPT-6.1 Terra，称其在低中 effort 下达到智能与成本的 Pareto 前沿，价格为 GPT-5.6 Terra 的一半或更低（$1/$5 每百万输入/输出 token）。
items.original_text: OpenAI has released GPT-6.1 Terra, pushing the cost efficiency frontier. It is the first Terra-class model since GPT-5.6, and is more intelligent for less than a third of the cost Pricing per token is half or less that of GPT-5.6 Terra - at $1/$5 per million input/output tokens vs $2/$12 for the previous model. Cache write has also halved, now at $1.25 per million tokens. Cached input is one quarter at $0.05 vs $0.20 per million tokens. Key takeaways: ➤ Pareto-optimal for Intelligence vs Cost at low and medium effort: At max effort, GPT-6.1 Terra gains 6 points in the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index over GPT-5.6 Terra, at less than a third of the cost per task ($0.40 vs $1.40). At lower effort levels the gain is larger, between 7 and 13 points. The low and medium effort levels are Pareto-optimal for cost efficiency, while the other effort levels sit behind the frontier. At max effort, the model scores 4 points below GPT-6.1 Sol and 10 points above GPT-6 Luna in the Intelligence Index. ➤ Pushes the Coding Agent Index cost efficiency frontier: With a score of 48 in the newly released Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index v2.0, the model is 6 points below GPT-6.1 Sol (54) and 17 points above GPT-6 Luna (31). The xhigh and low effort settings sit on the frontier of cost efficiency in the Coding Agent Index, while other effort levels are behind the frontier. ➤ 50 point drop in hallucination rate: GPT-6.1 Terra guesses 38% of the time when it does not know the answer to a question in AA-Omniscience, our private knowledge and hallucination benchmark. Previously, GPT-5.6 Terra's hallucination rate was 88%. This significant reduction in hallucination is coupled with a 2 point increase in AA-Omniscience accuracy - meaning the model simultaneously answers more questions correctly. ➤ 20 point jump in Terminal-Bench 4.0, small improvements across most evaluations: The model makes significant progress in the terminal-based agentic benchmark, Terminal-Bench 4.0, with a gain of ~20 points, now rivaling GPT-6.1 Sol at max effort. Gains across most other evaluations are smaller, for example, 5 points in GDP.pdf. With a score of 48 in the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index v2.0, GPT-6.1 Terra is 6 points below GPT-6.1 Sol (54) and 17 points above GPT-6 Luna (31). The xhigh and low effort settings sit on the frontier of cost efficiency. GPT-6.1 Terra shows a 50 point drop in hallucination rate, measured in AA-Omniscience. This is coupled with a 2 point increase in AA-Omniscience accuracy - meaning the model simultaneously answers more questions correctly. The model makes significant progress in the terminal-based agentic benchmark, Terminal-Bench 4.0, with a gain of ~20 points, now rivaling GPT-6.1 Sol at max effort. Breakdown of the individual evaluations in the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v4.3.2 Compare GPT-6.1 Terra with other leading models at: https://artificialanalysis.ai/models/releases/gpt-6-1-terra

items.title: Evan Armstrong 解析 Anthropic S-1：2 万亿美元估值是否成立
items.summary: The Leverage 创始人 Evan Armstrong 首次拆解 Anthropic 的 S-1 文件，评估其 2 万亿美元估值目标是否合理。核心数据包括累计融资 1411 亿美元、Q2 2026 收入 116 亿美元、约 900% 的净收入留存，以及 76% 的 2025 年收入来自约 1500 家年付费 10 万美元以上的企业客户。
items.original_text: Evan Armstrong used to write Napkin Math for Every, and since leaving he’s founded The Leverage , his own publication of clear-eyed analysis of where the tech market is heading. Today we’re teaming back up with him to co-publish his first cut at Anthropic’s S-1, and I loved getting to edit him again. If you like what you read, subscribe to The Leverage .— Kate Lee Was this newsletter forwarded to you? Sign up to get it in your inbox. The company whose AI writes marketing copy so bad it makes your eyes bleed is telling you that it is going to cure cancer. This is a ridiculous-sounding claim. Let me try again. The fastest-growing company ever, which has more than $100 billion in cash, which will soon control hundreds of billions of dollars’ worth of computing power, which has more than 11,000 customers paying it $100,000 a year, is telling you that it is going to cure cancer. This sounds, to me, marginally more reasonable. For three years we have understood Anthropic through a deluge of strategic leaks, hyperbole, FUD, jokes about shrimp welfare , memes, and way, way too many blog posts. Now, finally, we have cold, hard, SEC-approved data , through its S-1 filing. This document is absurd. Ridiculous. Stupid. It gives the details on a business the likes of which we have never seen before in the history of capitalism. I’ll give you lots of statistics today, but to start off: Anthropic has raised $141.1 billion since its founding in 2021. As of June 30 it still had $131.7 billion in cash and short-term investments. So the company has burned through less than $10 billion to get to a $16.8 billion quarter . In said quarter, it was even profitable on an operating basis. Again, ridiculous. Anthropic is reportedly targeting a $2 trillion valuation. Is this valuation equally ridiculous? What do you have to believe to accept this bet? Is it worth investing in this IPO? Let’s discuss. Revenue: The most absurd number ever printed Revenue increased from $376 million in Q1 2025 to $11.6 billion in Q2 2026. The third quarter of this year came in around $16.8 billion , though note that figure is press-reported; the S-1 leaves Q3 blank pending audit review. That is roughly $35 billion of trailing revenue for a company that did not exist six years ago. Yeesh. What impressed me most was net revenue retention (NRR). Anthropic reports it at approximately 900 percent as of September 30. In MBA-accessible English: The customers who were paying a year ago are now paying nine times as much. For context, the highest NRR any public software company has ever printed is Snowflake’s 189 percent in late 2019, on about $69 million of quarterly product revenue. The public software median is 110 percent . Anthropic did 900 percent on a $16.8 billion quarter. Again, yeesh. The definitions are not apples to apples (Anthropic’s metric excludes Pro and Max subscribers and counts only “qualified customers”), but still, no one has ever done this before. That said, don’t over-index on this number. I think of foundation models as being akin to Hollywood, not Silicon Valley SaaS. In Tinseltown, you are only as good as your next movie, and in the LLM game, you are only as good as your next model. The reason they grew ninefold this year is because Anthropic released a series of ever-greater Claude models over the past 12 months (from Opus 4.5 onward). The S-1 backs up my movie business mental model. Anthropic disclosed that models older than six months earn less than 20 percent of revenue. Versions released in the six months up to September 30 produced more than 80 percent of Q3 revenue. So frontier models are an asset with a six-month half-life. As the models themselves get better at making new models, I would expect that half-life to decrease over time. My second piece of evidence is how clearly the document illustrates Jevons paradox: As AI becomes cheaper and more efficient, people use so much more of it that total spending rises. Essentially, harder tasks have to cost less with each model release for the company to grow. The company says that every release “cuts cost per task 25 to 45%.” For example, after the Opus 4.5 price cut in November 2025, quarter-over-quarter growth went from 48 percent to 132 percent. Translation: Anthropic has to grow volume faster than it cuts price, forever, on a cost base that is contracted years in advance. My third piece of movie logic evidence is that Anthropic’s growth is already slowing from absurd to merely insane. The second quarter was 144 percent quarter over quarter; the third was about 45 percent. Part of that is the summer, when Fable met real competition from OpenAI and open-weight models for the first time. Part of it is cleanup: The company says 5 to 7 percent of revenue came from customers violating its usage policy, mostly labs distilling Claude, and it cut them off in August and September. ( Opus 5.5 appears to have at least partially restored the growth curve, but we’ll see in the next earnings if that is true.) To believe this company deserves to be in the trillion-dollar club, one of your biggest beliefs needs to be that it can produce better models than the rest of the world, essentially until the end of days. Who is actually paying? Despite starting off the S-1 with notes about how Anthropic is in the AGI business, for now, Anthropic is mostly in the Claude Code business. Claude Enterprise users who do not use Claude Code spend less than $75 a month. The top 5 percent of users, who do, spend about $1,500 a month. This is the single most important fact about Anthropic’s growth: The models happened to be the best at coding, the company built the application layer on top of them itself, and via the business strategy magic of vertical integration it captured the value instead of handing it to Cursor and Copilot. That hasn’t stopped the business from being a B2B monster. A few key points to highlight: This is a usage business sold to a few thousand companies, not a software company sold to 40 million users. The S-1 defines an enterprise customer as anyone paying $100,000 a year. By that definition, 76 percent of 2025 revenue came from about 1,500 organizations, and the other 24 percent came from roughly 40 million customers combined. The ratio has held between 57 percent and 90 percent every year since launch. Think of the consumer product more as a funnel and brand. All images courtesy of The Leverage. The real customer count is closer to 250 than 11,900. The 11,900 figure is the one the company leads with, and it grew eightfold in nine months, which is a legitimately absurd number. But the tiers are a power law. Each 10x step in annual spend cuts the customer count by about sevenfold, and the line extends cleanly to an implied 30 to 40 customers above $100 million a year. If you count every one of the 11,900 accounts at the bottom of its tier, the arithmetic floor is $5.15 billion. When you underwrite this company, you are underwriting roughly 250 relationships and the rate at which the next 1,650 climb into that group. Despite that, the concentration risk is not the one in the risk factors. No single customer accounted for more than 10 percent of total revenue for the nine months prior to the filing. The top five were about 25 percent of revenue over the period, falling from 36 percent in Q1 to 21 percent in Q3 while each of the five set a record. That trend is the single best number for the bull case in the filing. The problem is who the whales are. The reporting consensus is Cursor and GitHub Copilot , which the footnotes support in outline: Customers A and B were 12 percent each in 2025, and Customer C swung from 43 percent of revenue in 2023 to less than 10 percent to 11 percent in the first half of 2026. If that identification is right, the largest customers are coding products that sit between Anthropic and the end user, which have every incentive to route tokens to whichever model is cheapest this quarter, and whose owners (SpaceX and Microsoft, respectively) run their own model programs. The upside case is the mirror image. More than half the Fortune 500 pays Anthropic at least $100,000, and the filing says those companies spend less than 0.1 percent of their total expenses with it on average. The top 10 Fortune 500 accounts spend less than 1 percent. If the average Fortune 500 customer moved to where the top 10 already are, revenue from that cohort alone would grow eightfold. The bet at $2 trillion is that the power law keeps its shape while the whole curve shifts right. What is gross margin anyhoo? Surface-level analysts will likely laud Anthropic’s reported 85 percent gross margin. This would make the company a SaaS stock. However, while the company is using the SEC-accepted definition, this gross margin definition isn’t spiritually accurate. Cost of revenue, as reported, is the compute attributed to customer-serving workloads. But Anthropic says, in its own IPO document, that it runs compute as one fungible pool. The model a customer is buying today was trained with research compute six months ago, and all the billions spent training it will be obsolete six months from now. So to properly understand this company, I think you need to treat frontier training as the cost of producing the thing being sold. If you do that by including total compute and infrastructure spend, then the cost of goods sold is $8.9 billion and gross margin is 45 percent. On that number, Anthropic is more akin to a hardware business (which is not to its benefit). Anthropic enjoys software gross margins when serving customers while suffering hardware gross margins when it does the research necessary to stay relevant. And as we’ve already established, the second cost never goes away. The closest comparison is the Netflix content-amortization debate from 2015 to 2019, when the argument was whether original programming should be expensed or capitalized over five years. Here the content expires in six months. Unfortunately, we don’t get much more detail on the future cost of training models—most likely because Anthropic doesn’t know what it’ll be well enough to publicly commit to something. But in my conversations with researchers, most of them expect the cost increase to be logarithmic. While we’re on the income statement, a brief note on the fact you will see in every headline. Anthropic lost “$80.7 billion” in the first half of 2026. This is a nonsense number that isn’t worth worrying about. The actual operating loss was $693 million. The loss was driven by $72.4 billion of mark-to-market losses on Amazon’s convertible notes. The notes convert at the IPO, so the loss vanishes from the P&L the quarter after listing. (This is a rare case where an $80 billion loss could easily be interpreted as a buy signal.) The compute spend is absurd Current compute expense is about $22 billion a year, Q2 annualized. The contracts take that to roughly $120 billion a year next year and about $155 billion by 2028, most of it non-cancelable. Revenue, meanwhile, is consumption-priced and cancelable at will, and the five largest customers are mostly not on long-term contracts. Long-term debt being married to short-term revenue makes my stomach queasy. The S-1 spends a lot of time arguing that this spend isn’t a good bet. Anthropic has structured the financing program such that it separates data-center commitments (which have long lead times and bear a small share of cost) from accelerator commitments (short lead times, most of the cost), so the biggest checks get written closer to when demand is visible. To back up this plan, it dropped another shocking statistic, namely that this year, revenue grew 1,368 percent against 300 percent growth in compute. Additionally, demand has exceeded supply in every single period since Claude launched, so the risk the company has actually lived through is under-commitment, not over-commitment. All of these points are true, yet still, it all depends on the next model being as good as the last one and Anthropic having the vertically integrated app necessary to capture that value. Despite the big upcoming spending, the business has been remarkably efficient. The revenue per employee is $6.6 million on a trailing basis, up from $1.4 million a year earlier. Google is at $2.2 million. SpaceX, with xAI inside it, is at $1.4 million. So here is where we are. The most efficient scaling in the history of the industry, 900 percent net retention, 85 percent serving margins, $131 billion in the bank, and $800 billion of fixed obligations that the company can only meet if the next six models are as good as the last six. At $2 trillion, is that a buy? It depends, again, on whether you would trust Claude to cure cancer. The case for $2 trillion This section is for paid subscribers Subscribe to read the rest of this article. Start free trial Evan Armstrong is the founder of The Leverage , a newsletter that examines business strategy and power in tech markets.

items.title: SGLang 披露并修复 PD 分离服务中的跨请求 KVCache 竞态问题
items.summary: SGLang 团队与 Cloudflare 协调披露 2026 年 8 月 27 日至 9 月 9 日影响 Workers AI 上 @cf/zai-org/glm-5.3 的跨请求 KVCache 暴露问题。
items.original_text: On September 9, 2026, Cloudflare notified us of cross-request KV cache exposure in its GLM-5.3 deployment on Workers AI. We worked with Cloudflare to address the request-rejection path involved and strengthen related cache-lifetime handling in disaggregated serving. We are publishing this disclosure in coordination with Cloudflare and the researcher who reported the issue through Cloudflare’s HackerOne program. Cloudflare’s report covers its production incident and customer impact, and the researcher’s report (available soon) will describe the discovery and external validation. This post focuses on the underlying mechanisms, the changes we made, and guidance for SGLang operators. Read Cloudflare’s report here. Impact and affected deployments Cloudflare reports that the incident affected @cf/zai-org/glm-5.3 on Workers AI between August 27 and September 9, 2026. Its investigation found no other Workers AI model affected. Cloudflare’s investigation found that requests exceeding the prefill KV cache capacity could return content from another user’s session. For details on the incident’s scope and customer impact, see Cloudflare’s incident report. The issue occurred in disaggregated prefill/decode serving, where separate workers process the prompt and generate the response. The single-node rejection path returned an error instead. What happened Cloudflare’s deployment had a configured context length of 1,048,576 tokens, but its prefill KV cache pool could hold 681,280 tokens. A request could therefore fit the configured context window while exceeding the memory available to process it. In SGLang’s disaggregated prefill/decode path, a request marked for rejection could still proceed through the handoff. Decode could then read cache pages that had not been populated for that request. The configuration mismatch made the rejection path reachable. The admission fix described below ensures that a rejected request returns an error before entering the disaggregated handoff. It complements deployment checks that compare pool capacity with the configured context length. Cloudflare disabled public access to the model on September 9. It increased the prefill pool to accommodate the configured context window and deployed a Cloudflare-authored engine patch that returned errors for rejected requests. Cloudflare reports that it validated these changes against the researcher’s reproduction and its own canary-marker tests before restoring the model that evening. The upstream fix, #36988 , retires aborted requests when their final prefill result is processed. Follow-up change #38935 stops intake-rejected requests earlier, before they enter the disaggregated handoff, avoiding unnecessary work and delays. Alongside the admission fix, we worked with Cloudflare on how SGLang handles KV cache transfers when requests are interrupted. In prefill-decode (PD) disaggregated serving, an aborted request can still have RDMA writes in flight. If decode releases and reassigns the destination slots before those writes complete, the late writes can overwrite another request’s KVCache and corrupt its output. Cloudflare’s report also describes our joint work on related KV cache lifetime issues. The following sections explain the deferred-release mechanism, additional transfer safeguards, and integrity checks, along with our validation results and guidance for operators. Background In PD-disaggregated serving, the prefill and decode phases run on separate engines, and each request’s KVCache must move from the prefill engine into the decode engine’s memory pool. For performance, this transfer is asynchronous. Transfer engines such as Mooncake, NIXL, or MORI issue it as one-sided RDMA WRITE operations that stream KVCache chunks into pre-reserved destination slots while prefill computation is still in progress. Because the transfer is asynchronous, a request can die while some of its writes are in flight. Prefill can then drop the chunks still waiting in its software queues, but it cannot stop a write it has launched toward the destination, such as the chunk in progress at that moment. In earlier implementations, when a request terminated mid-transfer (a client disconnect, a timeout, a transport fault), decode returned its destination slots to the allocator at termination, without waiting for such a write to finish. If the allocator reassigned the slots before the write landed, the dead request’s KVCache landed in another request’s KVCache. In typical workloads the corruption was rare, although long contexts make it far more likely (see fact 4 below). Each occurrence was silent. The transfer reported success, and no component raised an exception or logged an error. A single contaminated slot derails an entire generation, because attention reads every position. As a result, a request asking the model to count from 1 to 15 comes back as an incoherent stream of unrelated tokens. We then set out to make the race reproducible on demand and to fix it end to end, from the transfer engine layer up to the serving engine. The Problem: When Is a KVCache Slot Actually Free? The failure takes four steps: A client disconnect, an admission rejection, or a transfer fault aborts request A mid-transfer while at least one launched write has not yet landed. Decode frees A’s KVCache slots at abort time. The allocator marks them free while the remote writer is still writing to them. The allocator hands those slots to victim request B. A’s launched writes land inside B’s KVCache, and B decodes on foreign keys and values with no error. These steps apply to any PD implementation that moves KVCache between engines with asynchronous DMA, push or pull, because each one has to decide when a slot is free. We diagnosed and fixed the family in SGLang. Figure 1: The race. The abort frees A’s slots while A’s launched writes are still landing; B inherits the slots and the late writes land inside its KVCache. Four facts about the system make each step possible. 1. The allocator can mark a slot free while writes to it are in flight. In PD disaggregation, the decode engine pre-reserves destination KVCache slots for each incoming request, and its allocator tracks them as allocated or free. But “free” has a second, hidden condition: A slot is safe to reuse only when no remote writer can still touch it . The bugs in this class come from the gap between these two definitions. Each one is a distributed use-after-free, where the dangling pointer is a write request sitting in a NIC queue on another machine. The fix makes the second condition explicit, observable, and bounded. 2. Launched RDMA work cannot be cancelled, for push and pull alike. SGLang’s KVCache transfer is push-based [3]. Prefill writes KVCache into decode’s memory, because prefill knows the moment it produces each chunk and can overlap transfer with ongoing computation, chunk by chunk. At and below the NIC, cancellation is hard to achieve without hurting availability. The RDMA API has no call that cancels an individual work request already posted to the NIC’s queue pair. Python cannot interrupt the transfer engine’s blocking C++ call (e.g., Mooncake’s batch_transfer_sync ) mid-call. If that call times out, its work requests stay posted with no completion accounting, so those writes may land at an unknown later time. One-sided RDMA WRITE bypasses the receiver’s CPU, so decode gets no signal for each write that it could wait on. The NIC also places data per packet: A write interrupted mid-flight still leaves a partially written prefix at the destination, so even the paths that look like cancellation can mutate destination memory. A pull-based design would not escape this. If decode issued RDMA READs instead, an abort arriving mid-pull would leave decode’s own posted reads landing in slots it just freed, because a posted READ is as impossible to take back as a posted WRITE. Under pull, the hazard also runs the other way: If prefill frees its source pages at abort time and the allocator reassigns them while a READ is still in flight, that read fetches another request’s KVCache into decode. Freed-then-reassigned slots corrupt the transfer at either end. Figure 2: The transfer stack below the Python scheduler. An abort can stop future chunks, but everything already handed to the C++ engine or the NIC is beyond recall, and the receiving CPU never sees the writes at all. 3. Complete liveness handling starts at the router but cannot end there. An abort is only safe when both halves of a P/D pair learn about it. A well-designed PD router cancels the pair together, so neither side waits out a 300-second timeout for a peer that is never coming. In sgl-router , #41612 builds the PD pairing on top of the abort-on-disconnect of #39461 . The pair shares one router-minted request id. A client disconnect aborts decode, a prefill failure drops the decode request so the engine aborts it, and prefill learns of the abort through decode’s engine-side ABORT notification. sgl-model-gateway pairs the same two events ( #19524 for disconnects, #29017 for prefill failures). Before that engine-side notification existed, a router that aborted only one side guaranteed the race: Decode released its slots while prefill, never told, kept pushing. Even a perfect router only narrows the window. The abort reaches prefill asynchronously, after some scheduling and network delay, and whatever the transfer engine already launched (an in-flight C++ call, posted work requests) continues regardless. The router decides who dies (abort orchestration), and the engine decides when memory is safe (drain correctness). 4. The race window scales with prefill context length. SGLang chunks transfers and overlaps them with prefill computation, so the exposure window spans much of the prefill itself. A short prompt is in flight for milliseconds. A 128K–1M-token context, at tens to hundreds of kilobytes of KVCache per token depending on the model, keeps writes in flight for seconds to minutes, across many chunks and many posted work requests. The tail after the abort grows with it. A long context means more chunks in flight and more work requests still draining at the moment the abort lands, so launched writes can keep landing well after the allocator has reclaimed the freed slots. Under memory pressure, aborting a long request makes a write-after-reuse the expected outcome. Long-context workloads are also the ones where clients time out and disconnect mid-request. Long contexts therefore widen the window, lengthen the post-abort tail, and raise the abort rate all at once, so this bug class surfaces as deployments move to long-context serving. Impact and Exposure The aborted-transfer race described here requires three conditions: PD disaggregation is enabled with a KVCache transfer backend (Mooncake, NIXL, MORI, or a custom CommonKVManager backend). A single-instance deployment without this cross-engine transfer path is not affected by this specific race. A request terminates mid-transfer (client disconnect, router cancel, timeout, transport fault, prefill failure, or hicache restore failure) while at least one of its writes is launched and not yet landed. The allocator reassigns the freed slots to another request before the launched writes land, which under memory pressure happens in milliseconds. Remove any one of the three and the corruption cannot occur. Within PD deployments, default configurations were affected from the v0.4.x line (early 2025), when PD disaggregation shipped with RDMA backends, until v0.5.21, or v0.5.22 for MORI. A separate variant with the same signature required decode-side hierarchical cache offload, which is not on by default (fixed by #24226 and #30899 ). Deterministic or probabilistic? In production the race is probabilistic, so operators saw occasional corrupted outputs that they could not reproduce. Once the window is held open, it reproduces on demand (our harness in the next section, and the community reproducer in #32564 ). A client can raise the odds on purpose by sending long-context requests and disconnecting mid-transfer, which maximizes the race window and abort rate. The client cannot choose the victim or the landing slots, and the flow runs one way. The aborted request’s KVCache lands in another request’s KVCache, and nothing flows back to the aborter. The realistic impact is therefore one-way cross-request leakage, in which fragments of the aborted request’s context can surface in another client’s output, as they did in our reproduction. The aborter learns nothing, but in multi-tenant serving this is a data-leakage concern as well as an integrity one. Can a deployer tell whether exposure already occurred? A deployer has no reliable way to tell, because the corruption leaves no error or log line. The opt-in PD checksum ( #39500 ) can catch some late writes (see PD Checksum). After upgrading, use the #41128 metrics to confirm the protection is working (see Recommended actions for operators). Deterministic Reproduction We needed to reproduce the race before we could claim a fix, so we built a harness that triggers it on demand on a 1P1D pair. An env-gated delay inside prefill’s send_kvcache holds a launched write in flight, --max-total-tokens 96 forces immediate slot reuse, and instrumentation logs every request’s slot range and every free-or-hold decision. With the window held open, the overlap appears every time: Decode frees request A’s slots [14..44] while its write is in flight, request B allocates [1..32] , and the two ranges collide on [14..32] . A software delay cannot make the write itself land late on a single P/D pair, because the transfer queue serializes writes to the same decode engine. To show wrong output , not only overlapping slot numbers, we copied the aborted request’s freed page over the overlap at the victim’s commit point, which is what a late write does. Without the fix, the victim’s output was garbage. With the fix, decode held the donor’s slots, the victim got fresh slots, and the output was identical to the baseline. The real late landing also reproduces end to end on live hardware once two prefill engines share one decode, so nothing serializes their writes. We ran it on a 2×H200 pair (Mooncake over RDMA) with the hold disabled. A one-sided abort freed the donor’s 430 slots, the victim preallocated [1..105] inside them, and the donor’s launched write landed mid-decode. The victim counted correctly up to 80, then its output turned into the donor’s prompt text: Another request’s KVCache, read back out of its generation. With the hold enabled and the same timing, decode logged hold, drain-ack, and release, and the victim waited for the release and then produced output identical to the baseline, byte for byte. The full recipe (harness patch, launch script, driver, and the observed outputs) is in a public gist . The Fix: Deferred KVCache Release Decode cannot cancel prefill’s launched writes, so it keeps the aborted request’s slots reserved for longer than those writes can keep landing: T_hold > t_abort_propagation + t_remaining_chunks + t_in_flight_call The fix is safe only if this inequality holds on every abort path. The rest of the design makes every abort path hold the slots (the left side) and bounds each term on the right (detailed in #44186 ). Waiting for completion also fits the hardware: Reliable-connection RDMA executes work requests in order, so “all writes drained” is a single completion-queue observation on the sender. Deferred Release We built the mechanism in three steps: Notify prefill on abort ( #27372 ). On a decode-side abort, decode sends ABORT to every prefill rank, and each rank drops every chunk still waiting in the software queue for that room. That cuts t_remaining_chunks to near zero. Without the notification, every remaining chunk of the transfer launches and lands, so the term covers the entire rest of the prefill. t_in_flight_call is a separate term for the call already executing when the abort takes effect. On Mooncake’s serial per-room queue, the notification leaves nothing beyond that call, while a backend that posts chunks asynchronously, like NIXL, can still have several launched chunks outstanding. Either way, launched work keeps writing; the notification stops only what has not launched. Deferred decode-side KVCache release ( #35049 , NIXL port #35360 ). On abort, decode holds everything the request owns instead of freeing it: its KVCache slots, its row in the request pool, and its metadata buffer entry. That makes writer liveness explicit. Each prefill rank tracks its outstanding work per room and counts chunks at dequeue, so a count of zero proves that nothing already dequeued is still in flight. Chunks still waiting in the queue are safe for a different reason: Prefill marks the room failed before it arms the ack, so the worker drops them at dequeue. The rank replies ABORT_ACK only when that count drains to zero. Decode releases only when every notified rank has acked (the positive drain signal) or when a timeout fires (the bounded fallback). The timeout is a practical backstop, not a proof. Its length (30 seconds by default in #35049 ) matches the transfer engine’s per-call budget, which starts before the abort, and on a healthy path every launched write lands well inside it. A call that times out on a degraded path can leave writes that the engine is still retrying, so prefill never acknowledges a failed call as drained ( #43719 ), and the release waits out the full timeout. Decode never inserts slots released this way into the radix tree; it quarantines a failed room’s KVCache and discards it unread. Capability gating and default-on ( #37454 , #41023 ). The hold only helps on backends that ack. It shipped as an opt-in with a per-backend gate and became the default in v0.5.21, once Mooncake and NIXL both supported the drain ack. In #35049 , all chunks for a room go to the same transfer queue, served by a single worker thread. That worker is the room’s only writer, and it sends ABORT_ACK itself rather than leaving that to the bootstrap thread. Decode counts acknowledgments from dummy ranks too; those ranks acknowledge immediately. Once all expected acknowledgments arrive, no prefill rank can still write to the slots. Room IDs are reused across requests, so decode creates a new ack tracker for each abort and ignores acks for rooms it isn’t tracking. #37077 later added generation tags to the messages themselves. We tested this on 2×H200 by aborting 132 requests mid-transfer through the hold path. There were no crashes, and every held slot was returned once its hold resolved. Figure 3: The fix. On abort, decode holds A’s slots instead of freeing them. Every prefill rank drains its launched writes and replies ABORT_ACK , and the slots are released on the last ack, in milliseconds. The timeout is a bounded fallback that can only lengthen the hold, never shorten it. Decode retains the slots until all required drain acknowledgements arrive or the release timeout expires. A missing acknowledgement makes decode wait for the timeout. Timeout-based release is safe only if outstanding writes have stopped by then; expiry alone does not confirm that they have drained. The mechanism holds slots only on the abort path (see Performance Impact). Even on the abort path, the hold costs nothing unless the pool is near exhaustion and an incoming request cannot allocate until those slots return; then it shows up as a short admission delay. A feature under development will cut this cost further: Decode will receive the KVCache into host memory first and copy it into VRAM only when the transfer is done and the request is about to start decoding. The hold will then occupy host memory instead of GPU KVCache capacity. Failed Mooncake Sends #43719 , merged on October 12, 2026, closes an early-release path in the Mooncake drain ack. Before it, if a submitted Mooncake send returned an error, prefill marked the room failed and still acked it as drained once decode’s ABORT arrived. An error from batch_transfer_sync does not mean the writes stopped: After a timeout, the slices keep retrying, and after a failed batch, other tasks can still be in flight. Decode freed the slots on that ack, and the leftover writes could land in another request’s KVCache. #43719 withholds the drain ack for any room whose KVCache, state, or aux send failed, so decode holds the slots until its release timeout. Every failed send now costs that hold, until Mooncake can report whether a failed batch has drained. #43719 is on main, for release in v0.5.22. Admission Fix Admission control starts at the router. A PD router sends each request to a prefill worker and a decode worker together, and decode cannot produce a token without prefill’s KVCache. If prefill rejected or failed a request, the decode half used to wait out its 300-second timeout while it held a decode slot, so a burst of prefill failures could pin many decode slots at once. #29017 in sgl-model-gateway and #41612 in sgl-router now drop the decode request as soon as prefill returns an error, and the decode engine aborts it within seconds. Inside the engines, #38935 , merged on September 16, 2026, retires a request that a worker rejects at intake when it enters either admission queue ( PrefillBootstrapQueue.add or DecodePreallocQueue.add ), before any handoff state exists. Before it, a rejected request still reported itself as live, so it completed a bootstrap handshake, reserved a metadata buffer, and ran a forward pass on a one-token stub; #36988 retired it only after that pass. If both workers reject a request, decode now returns 400 at once instead of timing out after 300 seconds. This keeps rejected requests out of the disaggregation handoff. Mooncake Transfer Batch Size Tuning Two settings guard a Mooncake transfer call. The first is Mooncake’s own MC_TRANSFER_TIMEOUT (30 seconds by default), which fails any batch_transfer_sync call that takes longer. A call that fails this way can still leave writes in flight (fact 2), which is why prefill withholds the drain ack after a failed send. The second is SGLANG_MOONCAKE_MAX_TRANSFER_BATCH_INDICES , added in #32758 (merged September 8, 2026), which caps the data volume, and with it the duration, of each call. At its default of 0, SGLang sends a chunk’s whole KVCache in one call, the efficient path. A positive value splits the transfer into ordered calls of at most that many indices, so a hung call strands at most one batch of posted writes, and the first failed call ends the loop before the remaining batches post. Smaller batches cost throughput and TTFT, so lower the limit only as an extra safeguard for extreme context lengths. In #32758’s tests, a single call for an 800K-token request carried 30 GB. SGLANG_DISAGGREGATION_DEFERRED_DECODE_KV_RELEASE_TIMEOUT then sets T_hold . A value of 60 to 120 s gives the hold a wide margin. A larger value adds little safety and multiplies held KVCache during abort storms. If releases fall to the timeout, held capacity is about abort rate × T_hold × pages per request, so size the decode pool for that product. PD Checksum #39500 , merged on September 16, 2026, adds an optional integrity check for the transferred KVCache, off by default. Prefill computes an Adler-32 checksum on the GPU, over contiguous regions and over indexed KVCache and state pages, and sends it with the final chunk. Decode records it when it commits the transfer and checks the received KVCache against it before the request joins a running batch, so it catches late writes that land before that point; the hold keeps later writes out of reused slots. Decode keeps the checksum across retraction. A mismatch aborts the request and increments the transfer-failure counter; in CI, a mismatch raises an error instead. Health-check requests skip the check. To turn it on, pass --disaggregation-enable-kv-checksum to both the prefill and decode engines; their KVCache layouts must match. The flag adds an optional metadata buffer. It stays off by default because every transfer pays for an extra GPU read of the KVCache and an extra synchronization point when flipped on. We also evaluated a commit-time check of the transferred length and declined it: The published length derives from the same prefill accounting that gates Success, so the two sides can only agree. Performance Impact Across 21 runs on 2×H100 (1P1D Mooncake, 1024 requests at concurrency 256, 7 repetitions per arm), throughput was statistically indistinguishable before the patch and with the feature enabled or disabled. All deltas were within ±2%, and every 95% confidence interval spanned zero. Five weeks before the default flipped, a separate 16-run sweep on 2×H200 measured the cost of defaulting the feature on at −0.38% (CI −2.12 to +1.36, not significant). On the abort path itself, the cost depends on the ack fast path. With it alive, a held request releases milliseconds after the drain; with it dead, every abort pays the full release timeout. Recommended actions for operators For PD deployments, we recommend the following: Upgrade. v0.5.21 protects Mooncake and NIXL deployments by default, for every failure kind. We have not backported this fix line to earlier release branches. MORI deployments, and the generation-tagged ack hygiene, need a build at or past the merge of #37077 (2026-10-03, in v0.5.22). In practice, cut the build past #41128 , merged twelve hours later the same day, so it also carries the release metrics described below. When prefill and decode use different acknowledgement formats, the drain handshake can fail and releases fall back to the configured timeout. A new decode drops generation-less acknowledgements from an old prefill, and an old decode receives no acknowledgement from a new prefill. In these cases, safe release depends on outstanding writes stopping within the hold period. Run a router that pairs aborts. Engine-side holds protect a deployment only after the abort reaches the engine. A router that cancels both halves of the pair (as sgl-router ’s PD mode does) is the first layer of defense. On v0.5.19 or v0.5.20 , set SGLANG_DISAGGREGATION_DEFERRED_DECODE_KV_RELEASE=1 on both prefill and decode servers. This enables the hold for decode-initiated aborts (the most common kind), though most releases wait out the timeout. On v0.5.20, also set SGLANG_MOONCAKE_MAX_TRANSFER_BATCH_INDICES ( #32758 ) and a generous SGLANG_DISAGGREGATION_DEFERRED_DECODE_KV_RELEASE_TIMEOUT (60–120 s), sized as described under Mooncake Transfer Batch Size Tuning. Neither replaces upgrading, because failure kinds other than decode-initiated aborts stay unprotected before v0.5.21. On current builds the defaults are correct, and the knobs add margin. Watch sglang:decode_deferred_kv_release_total{outcome} after rollout. The metric ships in v0.5.22 ( #41128 ). A healthy deployment releases almost all holds through drained . A timeout-heavy ratio means the ack path needs attention and every abort is waiting out the full hold. Conclusion These rules apply wherever KVCache moves asynchronously, whether between engines, memory tiers, or pipeline stages: Never free a slot an async engine may still touch. Hold until a positive drain signal or a bounded timeout. Make every degradation lengthen the hold. Ship each fix small enough that its regression test proves exactly one thing. If a PD deployment shows output corruption that these fixes do not explain, or anything that looks like this family, open an issue on sgl-project/sglang with the topology (prefill/decode parallelism, transfer backend, version), the request pattern around the incident, and the decode_deferred_kv_release metrics if available. The maintainers treat this class of report with priority. Acknowledgement We thank the reporting researcher for identifying the exposure, providing a reproducible report, and coordinating disclosure. We are especially grateful to Cloudflare, whose engineers shared the production context, developed the initial incident patch, and worked with us through the upstream fixes and hardening audit. We thank the following people for their work on these fixes: SGLang Community/RadixArk: Shangming Cai, Banruo Liu, Wenbo Jiang, Cheng Wan, Shiyang Chen, and many others Cloudflare: Kevin Flansburg, Kastan Day We also thank @AsterWang and @KastanDay , whose early PRs ( #24580 , #32564 ) called out this race and proposed holding pages before reuse. Pull Request List Router abort pairing: #41612 , #39461 , #19524 , #29017 Admission fix: #36988 , #38935 Abort notification to prefill: #27372 Deferred decode-side KVCache release: #35049 , #35360 Capability gating and default-on: #37454 , #41023 Ack fast path: #40645 , #41402 Hold on every failure kind: #41404 Failed Mooncake send never acks as drained: #43719 FakeKVReceiver regression fix: #41618 Generation-tagged acks and MORI support: #37077 Cross-backend protocol alignment: #35281 , #36612 Hicache retraction race: #24226 , #30899 Hicache restore rank consensus: #43562 Mooncake transfer batch size: #32758 PD checksum: #39500 Release metrics: #41128 Early proposals, reproducer, and audit (not merged): #24580 ( @AsterWang ), #32564 ( @KastanDay ), #38961 ( @kflansburg ) Reference [1] Mooncake: A KVCache-centric Disaggregated Architecture for LLM Serving. https://github.com/kvcache-ai/Mooncake [2] SGLang PD Disaggregation documentation. https://docs.sglang.io [3] Deploying DeepSeek with PD Disaggregation and Large-Scale Expert Parallelism on 96 H100 GPUs. https://www.lmsys.org/blog/2025-05-05-large-scale-ep/ Appendix The table below summarizes the issues and fixes discussed above, starting with request routing and moving through KV cache handling. Layer Problem Fix Router One-sided aborts, where decode dies and prefill keeps pushing (or vice versa, each waiting 300 s for a dead peer) The PD router cancels the pair: #41612 in sgl-router (on top of #39461 ); #19524 and #29017 in sgl-model-gateway Admission Requests rejected at intake still entered bootstrap, reserved buffers, and ran a stub forward Reject and clean up at the admission doors, before any handoff state exists ( #38935 , building on #36988 , which cleans up aborted requests after the forward pass) Stop new writes Prefill, unaware of a decode abort, keeps queueing chunks Decode-side abort notifies every prefill rank ( #27372 ) Hold until drain Launched writes cannot be cancelled Deferred slot release until per-rank drain ABORT_ACK or timeout ( #35049 , #35360 ) Keep the fast path alive Ack lost to a clear() race → every abort pays the full timeout Keep the ack target until outstanding writes drain ( #40645 ) One ack slot per room → MLA fan-out ranks (prefill TP < decode TP) never acked Fan the ack out to every decode peer the room knows ( #41402 ) Ack arrives before the decode tracker is armed → dropped Arm the tracker before sending ABORT ( #41402 ) Hold on every path The hold armed only for decode-initiated aborts; transport/prefill faults released at t=0 Defer on every failure kind ( #41404 ) Protocol hygiene A reused room id could consume a stale ack; MORI had no ack at all Generation-tagged ABORT / ABORT_ACK in the common layer; MORI opts into the hold ( #37077 ) Sibling pipes The hicache retraction path freed device slots under an active device→host offload copy, so poisoned KVCache persisted into the host tier Retraction waits for the offload to drain ( #24226 , #30899 ) Rank consensus TP ranks branched on the rank-local hicache restore status after the MIN-reduced KVCache poll. One rank’s failed restore desynchronized the group (queue-length mismatch, scheduler crash), and its admission accounting diverged one tick later Fold the restore outcome into the already-reduced KVCache poll, so every rank makes one decision ( #43562 ) Detect Corruption that slips past prevention is invisible Opt-in transfer checksums ( #39500 ); a commit-time length validation was evaluated and declined (see PD Checksum) Observe No way to tell if the ack fast path is alive in production Hold count, duration, and drained / timeout / error outcome metrics ( #41128 ) The middle rows came from a community audit. In the audit, published on September 11, 2026 ( #38961 ), @kflansburg found two more ways the race could reopen. The drain ack often failed to arrive, so releases fell back to the timeout. A fault that decode did not itself initiate never armed the hold, which reopened the original bug by another path. We closed both on main between September 22 and 28, 2026: The hold now arms on every failure kind, and the drain ack now reaches decode. The audit also flagged prefill’s own source pages, and our analysis showed that path was already safe, because those bytes can only land in slots the decode hold is quarantining. #43562 , merged on October 11, 2026, fixes a further finding, a rank-divergent HiCache restore. Disclosure Timeline Date Event 2026-09-09 Cloudflare notifies the SGLang maintainers of a cross-request KVCache exposure in production and shares follow-up safety checks in #38704 2026-09-10 SGLang maintainers meet with Cloudflare to agree on upstream fixes 2026-09-11 Hardening audit ( #38961 ) finds the ack fast path often falling back to the timeout in production shapes 2026-09-16 Admission fix ( #38935 ) and opt-in PD checksum ( #39500 ) merged 2026-09-22 → 09-28 Fast path restored ( #40645 , #41402 ); every failure kind defers ( #41404 ); default-on ( #41023 ); hicache fix ( #30899 ) 2026-10-02 v0.5.21 released, protected by default (Mooncake, NIXL) 2026-10-03 MORI and generation-tagged acks merged ( #37077 ); ships in v0.5.22 2026-10-11 Rank-consensus fix for decode HiCache restore merged ( #43562 ) 2026-10-12 Failed Mooncake sends no longer ack as drained ( #43719 ); ships in v0.5.22 2026-10-22 Failed NIXL and MORI sends no longer ack as drained ( #45973 ); ships in v0.5.23 2026-10-26 Coordinated disclosure by SGLang and Cloudflare.
